A shopkeeper earns a profit of Re 1 by selling one pen and incurs a loss 
of 40 paise per pencil while selling pencils of her old stock. 
(i) In a particular month she incurs a loss of Rs 5. In this period, she sold 45 pens. How 
many pencils did she sell in this period? 
(ii) In the next month she earns neither profit nor loss. If she sold 70 pens, how many pencils did she 
sell? 
By performing this activity students will  
1. Develop the concept of framing real life situation as well as trying to solve also

documents.chapter: -Lesson 6 Human Environment- Means of Transport and Communication
documents.text:
Lesson 6 explores the high adaptability of human beings as shown by numerous human 
settlements across the world, some even in difficult terrains like hills, deserts, and snowy 
regions. The students learnt about how humans stay connected for communication and trade 
through roadways, waterways, railways and technology. 
In this activity, we will further widen our learning about the human settlements to analyse how 
the growth of transport and communication in the present day has not provided equal benefits 
to men and women. 
At the end of the activity, students will be able to: 
• 
identify the inequality between men and women in using transport, internet and mobile 
phones 
• 
discuss how the inequality impacts the movements of girls and their participation in the 
workforce 
• 
discuss ways to improve transport and communication facilities for women 
How to conduct this activity: 
1. 
The teacher can start by asking the following questions to the students: 
1.1. What kind of transport problems do people face around you? 
1.2. Between men and women, who faces more problems? 
1.3. Do women have the same access to internet and mobile communication as men? 
1.4. What are the reasons for this unequal access to mobile phones? 
2. 
Discuss the fact sheet given at the end of the session plan and explain the points, if 
required. 
3. 
Next, discuss a few possible solutions to make transport safer for girls and 
women. The following points can be used as cues: 
- 
Promoting street markets, in deserted areas 
- 
Improved lighting in dark and deserted areas 
- 
Reserving seats and coaches for girls and women 
- 
Operating special buses only for women 
- 
Hiring more women to become drivers and conductors 
- 
Community sensitisation on women safety through posters and street plays 
- 
Digital training of girls and women on basic mobile phone usage 
- 
Installation of CCTV Cameras at bus stops and deserted streets 
- 
Live GPS Tracking of buses 
- 
Creation of Safety Apps

documents.text:
After Class Activity:- 
4. Poster Making: The teacher divides the class into groups of 5-6 students and asks each 
group to prepare a poster on ‘Making Transport Safer for Girls’ in the space provided 
below the fact sheet. 
5. Mention that a few groups will be invited to present their posters during the next recap 
session. 
 
 
KEY MESSAGE: 
Lesson 6 - Human Environment Settlements, means of transport, Communication and 
Trade - Fact Sheet - Status of Women in India 
1. Ideally, everyone should be able to move around freely, no matter their gender. 
However, in reality, men have more freedom to be out in public than women do. 
2. This is because of strict gender rules that say women should stay at home while men 
can go out. Safety is also a big issue. Most public spaces and public transportation are 
dominated by men. Women often feel unsafe because of harassment and violence, 
which limits their ability to move around and use public transportation. 
3. Access to safe and convenient transportation can help women be more productive and 
support gender equality. 
4. The internet and technology have changed the world and made life easier for many 
people. However, in India and around the world, not everyone has access to the 
internet and technology like mobile phones. Women and girls have even less access to 
these tools. Many people believe that the internet and mobile phones might "corrupt" 
young girls and women, so men in the family often control their access to these 
technologies. 
5. In many families, fathers and husbands make most of the decisions. They often decide 
that women and daughters do not need their own mobile phones. 
6. Early marriages and the belief that marriage is the most important thing for a woman 
lead parents to not prioritize education for their daughters. This causes many girls to 
drop out of school. 
7. Strict gender rules also affect women’s participation in the workforce. Women are 
often paid less than men for the same job and face restrictions on their movement and 
work due to safety concerns at night.

The Gymnastic Clock 
                                                                             M C Davies 
Main innovative pedagogies are:  
1. Warm up activity 
2. Poetry escape room 
3. Entice them with music 
4. Video play 
5. PPT for grammar 
6. Recitation  
7. Use of picture books 
8. Worksheets 
 
The above activities are come under the following 5’E methods. 
ENGAGE  
 
1. Warm up activity. 
                  Teacher asks the history of clock and collects information about the        
uses of clock from the students. 
 
EXPLORE 
 
1. Poetry escape room 
A poetry escape room is the most engaging and fun way to introduce 
or review poetry with your students. The teacher takes some pieces of 
every 2 lines in the poem and hides behind the walls in a classroom. 
Students can search and collect sheet of papers. Finally, they arrange 
the papers in a sequence order to make a meaningful poetry.
documents.subject: II Language English

documents.text:
2. Entice them with music 
Teacher better to begin the gymnastic clock poetry with music which 
students love it. Music is poetry, it sets a positive atmosphere. 
Analyzing music as poetry can be powerful and memorable learning 
experience. 
EXPLAIN 
 
1. Video play 
Teacher can show the DSERT’s video of the gymnastic clock poetry 
which runs under vidyagama programme. Students will come to know 
the importance of exercises which keeps our body healthy and realizes 
to build exercises in our daily schedule. 
 
2. PPT for grammar 
PPT can be shown for glossary, rhyming words and to find the figures 
of speech which helps to appreciates the poetry.  
 
EXPAND 
1. Recitation
documents.subject: II Language English

documents.text:
Poetry recitation and memorizing is a fun activity that you can engage 
your students to achieve outcomes of the poetry the gymnastic clock 
 
2. Use of picture books 
Children’s picture books are gold mines for poetry. Prepare a book 
using some pictures of exercises, clocks, poet’s image, animations 
along with poetry. Read a book to the entire class or pass out to 
different small groups and have them to analyze an aspect of the 
poetry. 
 
EVALUATION 
 
1. Worksheets  
 
Worksheet 1 
How do I know if I am active enough? Instruct students to perform these 
activities.

exercises which keep our body healthy.

UNIT 2: AWARENESS(POEM)           
 
 Activity 1: Experiment 
  
Procedure: Teacher enables children to do an experiment by 
their own to see how plastic makes earth barren land by 
tossing plastic things on the soil surface. Children have to 
take 2 pots filled with soil (and some seeds if necessary). 1 
pot covered with plastic cover another one should keep open 
to air. Have to pour water daily on the pots. 
      Observe after one week, one pot and its soil looks healthy 
(seeds may germinate) but another pot became dry . 
 
Materials required: 2 pots, soil, water, seeds, plastic bags, 
etc.. 
 
Time duration:  a week or more 
 
Outcome of the activity: 1. Children will be able to get an 
idea about the necessity of air, water and soil on earth. 
2. Children will be able to learn how plastic affects soil 
fertility and made it barren land.

documents.text:
Activity 2 : Slide show 
  
Procedure: Teacher makes children to watch a video clip 
or a slide show which shows air, water and soil pollution 
and let them to decide what they to take safety measures to 
save air , water and soil. Teacher asks some questiond like 
what are the things which pollute air, water and soil?

CONTENT OUTLINE 
 
Part-I   
 
Competency-based Education 
Module 1  
 
Understanding Competency-based Education 
Part-3   
 
Why Competency-based Education is Important and Needed? 
 
 
 
1. 
A quote by Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam 
o “Educationists should build the capacities of the spirit of inquiry, creativity, 
entrepreneurial and moral leadership among students and become their role model.” 
 
2. 
A shift from traditional education system to a competency-based education system 
Traditional education system- 
o Follows 'one-size fits all approach' for students 
o Advancement is based on seat-time than Mastery in learning 
o Does not focus on building competencies required for life-long learning   
 
3. 
Need for competency-based education 
o Lifelong learning 
o Empowered and inclusive culture of learning 
o Timely and differentiated instruction and support 
o Pedagogical principles aligned to meet needs and goals of students 
o Transparency with clear and explicit expectations 
 
4.  
Benefits of competency-based education 
A student-centered approach 
Gives flexibility to students  
Focuses on achieving proficiency 
Provides timely support and feedback to students 
Promotes one-to-one learning 
Has a transparent Grading system

documents.text:
Steps for Meditation Practice 

Objective of the Meditation Practice 
 
To build and strengthen ability to be calm and relax one’s mind and body 
To re-energize self by connecting to experiences that help to feel safe and secure. 
 

Select a Comfortable Corner 
 
Find a comfortable corner in the house; it could also be your balcony, lawn, and terrace full of  
natural surroundings or a quiet serene corner of one of your rooms where you could spend time  
with yourself. 

Meditation Position 
 

You may choose to sit on a cushion or a mat cross legged (Aasana position) or sit on a  
chair where you would feel comfortable calm and at ease. 

On cushion, mat or chair feel the comfort from the sense of touch to the cushion or the  
floor. 

Sit straight shoulders broad back upright and relaxed. 

Head comfortably resting on the spine with chin tucked in slightly. 

Keep your face and jaw relaxed.
documents.subject: Training

documents.text:

Eyes closed or open as you may feel comfortable. 

While you prepare for your meditation sitting position, check your body from head to  
toe for any signs of discomfort. In case of any discomfort, open your eyes and adjust  
yourself unless you feel comfortable. 
Please note:-You are requested to not practice in case you are not feeling well in the meditative position 
or if there is any pain in your body 

Breath (5-10 min) 
 

Once you have gained the comfortable posture, take slow deep breath through your  
nostrils. 

Feel the air passing through your lungs to your belly. 

Release your breath slowly. Try 3 cycles of breathing in and breathing out. 

With each breath in, feel calm, positive and smile. 

With each breath out, feel as if you are releasing all the negativity, anxiety and stress  
inside. 

Start with 3 cycles, and then do 5 and 7 as you get comfortable with the practice. 

Calling to Mind a Positive and Joyful Experience (15-20 min) 
 

Once you come to your natural breathing rhythm, try recalling any positive experience that has  
helped you feel safe, loved and cared for. You could also think about a place, a book or any real  
or imagined place or situation that has helped you in difficult times and made you feel safe and  
comfortable. 
 

Try to recall the details of the experience and notice how you are feeling. What was so beautiful  
about the experience? What made it such a beautiful experience? Was it the environment? Was  
it their smile, their care, their conversation, their quiet presence their encouragement or their  
help. 
 

Stay and Focus on the beauty, kindness of the moment for few minutes. 
 

Try to reflect if the care, the help, the support your received, if that practiced by you would help  
you and others.
documents.subject: Training

documents.text:
Closure (5-7 min) 
 

Towards the end, reflect if you developed any skill or insight. 

Dedicate any benefit you received out of this practice for the well- being of others in the  
world. 

Focus back on your breath, breathing in calmness, positivity and smile and breathing out  
worries stress and negativity. 

Slowly become aware of the contact with the floor, cushion mat chair. 

As you feel comfortable slowly open your eyes and smile. 
 
 
Share or Journal 

If you are practicing with a colleague or a friend, if possible share your experience and  
listen to others experiences. 

If practicing alone, keep a Practice Journal log, and write few lines how your experiences  
was. (Sample questions given below) 

You can share the journaled experiences in your learning communities for further 
development of the practice 
Individual Practice Reflection Questions – 
 

How was I feeling before the practice? 

How do I feel now after the practice? 

How long could I sit for practice? 

Did I feel any discomfort in the sitting positions? 

Was there any discomfort in recalling the experiences? 

How much have you improved from your last practice? 

What variations have you tried? Has variation helped? 
 
Important for individual Practice 
 
1.
Start with guided meditation if possible using the recordings. 
2.
In case you are not comfortable using guided meditation recordings, please listen to the steps or  
read the instructions and then practice all the steps 
3.
Break the steps and practice one step at a time in case you feel you cannot do all together for eg 
– Breathing cycles to gain comfort level and then add Calling to mind Joyful and Positive  
Experience
documents.subject: Training

documents.text:
4.
Practice in silence 
5.
Acknowledge if the mind is wandering and bring it back gently. 
6.
Practice as per your available time during the day – whenever you get time – you can start with  
15 min and increase it to 30-40 minutes 
7.
Allow the practice to develop by giving it time daily. In case you miss in the morning, try doing it  
before sleeping. 
8.
Make notes or journal your reflections

SUNDIAL: A sundial measures the time of the day by the change in
position of shadow due to the change in the sun’s position. The sun rises
in the morning and changes its position throughout the day, due to the
rotation of the earth. At many places, huge sundials have been constructed. In
India, famous sundials have been constructed at Jantar Mantar in Delhi and
world’s largest sundial at Jaipur, Rajasthan.

SAND CLOCK: Sand clock (fig. 13.6 (a)) also known as hour glass uses
flow of sand from one bulb to the other to measure time.

WATER CLOCK: Water clock (fig. 13.6 (b)) uses the time taken by water
to drip from the upper vessel to the lower vessel in certain interval of time.

Fig 13.6 Some Ancient time measuring devices

The ancient devices for measuring time were not suitable for measuring shorter
time periods like minutes and seconds. So, modern clocks and watches were discovered
to measure shorter time intervals. These clocks and watches have electronic devices
to operate them and are based on the principle of periodic motion. A motion which
repeats itself at regular intervals of time is called periodic motion. The modern
clocks are very much accurate than the earlier clocks. A simple pendulum is the
most important device used for periodic motion.

13.6 Simple Pendulum :

A simple pendulum is a heavy mass suspended by a thread from a rigid
support, say a stand. The point of suspension is O in figure 13.7.. The heavy
mass, say a bob should be free to move to and fro about its mean position. The
heavy mass or bob is a metallic ball and is suspended by a thin elastic thread
from a rigid support. When it is at rest, its position is called the mean position
(position B in figure). The to and fro motion of the simple pendulum is called
periodic or oscillatory motion. It has two extreme positions (Position A and C).
The to and fro motion of bob of simple pendulum from mean position B to
extreme position C and back to extreme position A then back to mean position

LET'S TRY TO ANSWER THIS QUESTION
Q. Look at the multiplication pattern below.
HOW DID STUDENTS PERFORM?
WHAT IS THE MISTAKE?
Students are not able to understand that the sign
of the product of negative integers with positive
integers depends on the number of negative
integers in the product.
LET'S CORRECT THIS MISTAKE
Students should be given clarity on how ‘-‘ multiplied by ‘-‘ results into a ‘+’ and how this is different from ‘-‘
added with ‘-‘. Properties and operations on integers can be very confusing for students especially when they
encounter more than one sign with a number for example: 2 + (-4) x 5 etc.
Once they are convinced of this, investigate if they know the properties of integer operations like commutativity
and associativity. Use these to help them extend the rule. The product of 3 negative integers can be considered
as a negative integer times the product of two negative integers, that is a negative integer times a positive
integer and hence a negative integer. Similarly the product of 4 negative integers (or any even number of
negative integers for that matter) can be grouped into products of pairs of negative integers. Each pair will
evaluate to a positive integer, and hence the product evaluates to a positive integer.
When we do this kind of pairing for a product consisting of an odd number of negative integer, one negative
integer remains that cannot be paired off. The product of the negative integers that can be paired off, evaluates
to positive. Together with the one that has not been paired, the product becomes negative. You may
demonstrate this with a number of examples. Thus help them see that a product consisting of an odd number of
negative integers is negative and even number of negative integers is positive. It is NOT the size of the negative
integers that matter, but the number of negative integers in a product.
LET'S UNDERSTAND WHERE THE
MISTAKE IS HAPPENING...
This question tests whether students are able to
apply the knowledge of property of multiplication
of integers. 
Students who have chosen option B (36.4%) have
correctly answered the question. Students who
have chosen option C (26.1%) and D (20.4%) have
associated even number with a positive product. 
 They seem to have got confused with the fact
that multiplication of minus sign for even number
of times results into a positive product. Students
who have chosen option A (11%) have probably
guessed the answer.
1 × (-1) × 2 × (-2) × 3 × (-3) × 4 × (-4)............

Answer knowledge, understanding, application and diagrammatic 
skill based questions based on the topic. 
 
ATTITUDES AND BELIEFS – Students will be able to  
 
Develop citizenship by visualizing and observing day to day phenomena 
and present it in form of a skit to sensitize others. 
 
Transaction 
Methodology 
(The teacher can

Transaction would proceed in the following manner- 
Active Learning- Frayer Model on Electric Current (Critical Thinking) 
 
Group Learning- The class will be divided into eight groups. Jigsaw 
Expert Group: The group will be given worksheet the two effects of 
electric current. 
Learning Group: Students will teach each other the heating effect of 
electric current and magnetic effect of electric current.. (Communication, 
Collaboration) 
  
Differentiation- The students in groups of 8 will be demonstrating the 
magnetic effect of electric current. (Character, Communication) 
 
Questioning- Multiple level questions- Teacher will prepare a list of 
question about electric current and its effects and will ask these questions 
after discussion. (Critical Thinking, Communication) 
 
Brain Storming-The class would start with a discussion on what the 
students have already learnt in the previous classes and hence what is it that 
they would learn now. They would also be told the significance of the topic 
that they would be studying. 
 
Introduction of the topic- PPT and Digital Content would be shared. 
 
Facilitation of content 
The facilitator will enable the learners to understand the fundamental 
concept of Heat. 
He/ She will compare and contrast different modes of transfer of heat. 
 
Approaches 
The facilitator should apply some or all the approaches while administering 
the teaching learning process. 
 Didactic Approach 
 Summarizing Approach 
 Feedback Approach 
 
Techniques to be used: 
 Quiz

ATTITUDES AND BELIEFS – Students will be able to  
 
Develop citizenship by visualizing and observing day to day phenomena 
and present it in form of skit to sensitize others. 
 
Transaction 
Methodology 
(The teacher can 
use the 
mentioned 
techniques, 
wherever 
applicable, and 
can use any 
other too.)  
Transaction would proceed in the following manner- 
Active Learning- Frayer Model on light. (Critical Thinking) 
 
Group Learning- The class will be divided into eight groups. Jigsaw 
Expert Group: The group will be given worksheet spherical mirrors 
Learning Group: Students will teach each other the concave and convex 
mirror. (Communication, Collaboration) 
  
Differentiation- The students in groups of 8 will be demonstrating the 
image formation by concave and convex lens. (Character, 
Communication) 
 
Questioning- Multiple level question- Teacher will prepare a list of 
question about light and its phenomenon and will ask these questions after 
discussion. (Critical Thinking, Communication) 
 
Brain Storming-The class would start with a discussion on what the 
students have already learnt in the previous classes and hence what is it that 
they would learn now. They would also be told the significance of the topic 
that they would be studying. 
 
Introduction of the topic- PPT and Digital Content would be shared. 
 
Facilitation of content 
The facilitator will enable the learners to understand the fundamental 
concept of Heat. 
He/ She will compare and contrast different modes of transfer of heat. 
 
Approaches

the teaching learning process.

Theme Neighbourhood
Prose : The Eyes Have It (Ruskin Bond)

Poem =: The Solitary Reaper (William Wordsworth)

This unit is about people living in our neighbourhood. People of different castes, religion and
professions are living around us. Every human being is unique and we see people having special
qualities all around us. Even a farmer is as important as a soldier. The present prose and poem
motivate our learners to accept the qualities of all people and try to make their lives beautiful.

The prose chosen for this unit is about having sensitivity towards people who are differently
abled and feel their emotional and mental states. This message has been presented well in the
story ‘The Eyes Have It’ by Ruskin Bond. After explaining each sense group, interact with the
students to check their comprehension.

The poem chosen for this unit is about a young girl reaping and singing all by herself in the
fields. Through this poem, learners should be able to appreciate the beauty of natural and simple

things.

Improving Listening and Speaking Skills:

Speaking activities are to be focussed and practised through the given exercises, ‘Read and
speak’ in relation to the text and theme. The focus should be on the achievement of learners being
able to talk about their experiences in dialogue form using grammatically correct sentences. The

‘Discuss and sing’ section is aimed at creating appreciation for traditional folk songs.

Improving Reading and Writing Skills:

Reading and writing activities are to be focussed and practised through the given exercise ‘Think
and write’ in relation to the text and theme. The focus should be on the development of writing
skills of the learners. They should be able to write about the conversations given in the story and
also a short paragraph on ‘ A day in the life of a farmer’ at the end of this unit.

Encourage and guide the learners to think, discuss, reflect and make a list of people who have
excelled in different fields inspite of being physically challenged given in ‘Project’ section.
Similarly encourage them to go through the ‘Read for knowledge’ section for additional
information and general knowledge related to a visually challenged singer of Jharkhand- Tumpa

Kumari.

Improving Vocabulary

For improving the vocabulary, expose the learners to new words given in the text, ‘Know
the words’ section and also by going beyond the text for supporting the learners to use
these words appropriately in their own language. The special vocabulary feature focussed
in this unit is infinitives and making new words from root words which are given in ‘Word

power’ section.

Improving Functional Language
For developing the communicative and functional language, explain the grammar items through
appropriate examples and contexts preferably in relation to the text or by going beyond the text
as given in ‘Language in use’ section. Support the learners for using these language items in thei
language. The focus of this unit is to identify and use proper conjunctions.

used after subject in sentence.

Negative sentence
+ Subject + has/have + not
+ 3rd form or past participle of ve
For example : / have not taken my meal
Interrogative sentences
+ Has/have + subject + 3rd form ofverb or past participle + o
For example : Have you taken your meal?

Sciences
1. 
The field of Learning Sciences
o
Interdisciplinary field
o
Implications for all aspects of school design and pedagogy
2.
Seven cornerstones of the field of Learning Sciences 
o
Learning is an activity carried out by the active engagement of the learner. 
o
Learning does not occur through a fixed progression of age-related stages. 
o
Learning is a dynamic interaction of cognition, emotion and motivation. 
o
Learning process is enhanced through effective feedback. 
o
Learning is shaped by the way information is processed and transferred into 
long-term memory. 
o
Optimal learning and mastery of new skills take place when new information is 
associated with an already existing knowledge. 
o
Learning is a social process that takes place in a socio-cultural context.

  Concept map 
 
 
 
  Synopsis: 
1. Neighbour - People living in nearby horses are neighbours. 
2. Neighbourhood- The area around a house is called neighbourhood. Every neighbourhood 
has a few facilities that make our lives more comfortable like park, temple, river, and field. 
3. Sides- Front, back, left and right are sides. They tell us the locations of a place or thing. 
4. Directions-Directions help you know where things are. North, South, East, and West are the 
main directions. 
5. Corners- The place between any two directions is a corner. 
6. Boundaries- The limits of any area, building or village are called boundaries. 
7. Courtyard- A courtyard is like a special area surrounded by buildings or walls. It's often 
open and can have plants or a place to play.  
8. Landmark- A landmark is an object or a feature of a landscape or town that has importance 
or makes a place easily recognizable. 
9. Map - Map is a representation or drawing of a place. 
10. Symbol- Representation of landmarks. 
11. Celestial body - a natural object outside of the Earth's atmosphere. For example- the moon 
and the sun. 
12. Sun - the star around which the earth orbits. 
13. Moon - the natural satellite of the earth, visible (mainly at night) by reflected light from the 
sun. 
14. Star - A star is an exploding ball of burning gas held together by gravity. Our sun is a star!

documents.text:
Food is the single strongest lever to optimize human 
health and environmental sustainability on Earth.  
The Lancet Commission (2019) . 
1
In other words, what we put on our plate has a direct impact on both our bodies and on 
the bio-diversity of our planet . The current situation of the pandemic has highlighted the 
2
need to focus on the links between the food we eat, how we source it and how we are 
inter-connected to our environment. 
This unit is linked to the learners' own context of what they eat and what this does to their 
body. It is easy to carry out with no complicated technical requirements or materials. It is 
multi-sensory and multi-disciplinary. This unit was created for grade 7 but it can be 
adapted to younger or older classes by choosing age appropriate concepts to be learnt. 
For example, older classes can study the economics of food chains, the impact of 
genetically modified food on our health and environment etc. (For this, see videos and 
read books by Dr Vandana Shiva, founder of Navdanya movement). At Mahatma Gandhi 
International School (Ahmedabad), the Café Project has been running since 2001, across 
the different classes from kindergarten to grade 12. In 2016, the Cafe project became part 
of the primary school education in Finland. 
Different cognitive competencies can be covered such as measurements, ratio and 
proportion, weight and volume, decimal, fractions, percentage, calculation of profit and 
loss, estimation and standardisation of the recipe etc. in Mathematics. Arts and 
technology can be integrated with work on posters, graphics, menu cards. collage work 
etc. Similarly in Sciences, students can learn about different components of food, a 
balanced diet, states of matter, physical and chemical changes, use of simple machines in 
the kitchen etc. In languages too, writing recipes, hosting a food show, writing a food 
review blog etc can be done. Many skills are developed for critical thinking, awareness of 
the environment and self-awareness as well as life skills such as collaboration, 
communication etc. 
Food is also linked to culture, to diverse festivals and these links can be explored. The 
proposed activities are just a glimpse of what is possible using a coherent pedagogy. This 
unit uses the Generated Resources Learning (GRL) methodology developed by Dr Anju 
Musafir-Chazot and Dr Chazot. This is an experiential learning methodology that 
promotes a sustainable pedagogy by using available resources and daily objects. 
  https://eatforum.org/content/uploads/2019/07/EAT-Lancet_Commission_Summary_Report.pdf

CYCLE 1: Learning about the food pyramid
1.Expressing Notion - Starter activity and group bonding  
• Each child pretends to eat a particular dish and mimes the action in an exaggerated way. 
They walk around pretending to eat and are instructed to ‘offer’ their imaginary food to a 
friend. Each child mimes sharing the food with at least 10 other classmates. 
02. Immediate feedback 
• In pairs or sub-groups, they discuss the different kinds of food shared. 
03 Exploring and Researching  
• Children see a video on different types of macro and micronutrients found in food and 
look at the food pyramid. They write a short note on important points from the video.  
• Students can open their snack boxes and in groups of 6/8 will categorise them according 
to different food groups like carbohydrates, proteins, fats, fibre, vitamins, etc.  
04 Immediate Reflection 
• Children discuss what kind of food are they generally consuming. Which category 
comes up more often, why? 
05 Creation 
• Flash a picture of the food pyramid on the projector or through a chart paper. Students 
guess which food was seen where on the pyramid. This is a good activity for visual 
concentration and recall and can be done a few times. 
• At this stage, the teacher can give a handout or lesson that they can read together and 
discuss. They can even make questions/puzzles on the handout in groups of 4. Other 
groups can solve it in teams and by turns. 
• In small groups, children draw or create a sculpture of an ideal food pyramid according 
to them and display their work. Here, they can use any medium – paper, collage, paint, 
recycled materials, clay etc. 
06 Feedback 
• Ask each sub-group to share with another sub-group. They give each other feedback on 
the food pyramid created, stating its strengths and weaknesses (Example: availability 
whether local or not, cost factor, health benefits etc). 
07 Reflecting on learning experiences 
• Children reflect on all the activities and write what, how and why each activity was 
done. 
©Anju Musaﬁr-Chazot, Anita Shah & Komal Saksena, Mahatma Gandhi Interna/onal School, Ahmedabad. !3

08 Feedback 
• There is an overall feedback shared about what they learnt and how they felt. 
Home activity: 
a.Record what kind of food they eat at home for a week- breakfast, lunch, snack and 
dinner.  
b.Collect the labels of foods that they enjoy eating or drinking. For this, they can even 
collect the empty packets (ex: juices, colas, biscuits, etc). They get it to school and display 
these in the classroom.

CYCLE 2 : What am I eating? 
01 Starter activity 
• Children sit in different corners and draw the food they eat the most often. All the 
drawings are mixed up and each child guesses who drew which drawing.  
• Once they have guessed all the names, each child takes back her or his own drawing.  
• In groups of 6/8, they categorise the drawings in different ways. For eg, based on taste, 
texture, colour, healthy, unhealthy, street, etc. 
02 Immediate feedback 
•They come and present their categories with explanation. 
03 Exploring and researching (learner context) 
• They are asked to bring food packets or labels from home (a couple of days notice is 
given). They analyse food labels and categorise them in different ways. For example:  they 
analyse the sugar content in juices and soft drinks and make a chart representing the sugar 
content found in them.  
• They understand the importance of a balanced diet and watch videos explaining the 
diseases caused due to unbalanced food. 
• Experiments are performed where they test for starch, proteins and fats in the lab using 
common foods.  
04 Immediate reflection 
• They reflect on their own eating habits. Is their diet balanced or are they eating too 
much of a particular food item?  
05 Creation (Art work, collage) 
• They make a collage of healthy and unhealthy foods by using the labels, from 
magazines, newspapers, etc.  
• They create word search using new vocabulary learned during the lesson. 
• They can also create a list of foods they eat according to different food groups. They can 
further statistically represent which food group was eaten more by them by making bar 
graphs. 
06 Feedback 
• In groups they create charts on different food groups and importance of balanced diet, 
present their work and give feedback. 
07 Reflecting on their learning experiences 
•They reflect on their learning. What is the impact of the food they eat? Do they need to 
make changes in their food habits? 
08 Feedback 
They share the insights gained with each other. 
©Anju Musaﬁr-Chazot, Anita Shah & Komal Saksena, Mahatma Gandhi Interna/onal School, Ahmedabad. !5

CYCLE 3: From recipe to the plate – Running a cafe 
(This can be made simple such as making lemonade/bhel/salad/ for a younger class) 
01 Starter activity/Group formation 
• Students are asked to think of an action that happens in a café restaurant and choose to 
play a role (it can be a chef, a client, a waiter etc) and mime it while walking in space. 
When the initiator says ‘stop’, they stop and guess what the action represents. 
• Different dry spices/fresh aromatic herbs can be brought and put in numbered paper 
cups that are closed with paper taped on it. Make a few pricks on it to allow the fragrance 
to come through (Ex: Fresh coriander/mint/cardamom, lemon/ etc). Pass around the paper 
cups so that each student can smell and guess the spice/herb. After that, we can work on 
their sense of taste too with sugar, lemon, salt etc but the students must have their eyes 
closed or be blindfolded! For this they can be in pairs and one student takes a spoon and 
puts in the palm of the other child who can guess from the texture, smell it and then taste 
it to guess the item. We suggest that students can do this mindfully, quietly with calm, 
relaxing music playing in the background. Another extension is also to put different 
vegetables in small feely cloth bags and pass it around for students to guess the vegetable. 
• Students are asked to work in groups of 4/6, and to enact the process of making a dish, 
step by step without speaking. Each group gets a chance to perform and others guess each 
step and the dish. 
2.Immediate feedback 
• Students discuss which the importance of different senses in cooking and eating. 
Which sense is important to them? The visual appeal of a dish? The taste or the smell? 
Or is each very important?  
03 Exploring and researching (learner context) 
• Students explore recipes of dishes they would like to make. The students can take a 
survey of other classes giving them options of the dishes they as a class can make. This 
will give the groups an idea of the exact number of plates they will be preparing. 
• They then decide a recipe that follows a balanced diet. Students are asked to create 
those dishes using appropriate materials, ingredients and recipes.  
• Now in groups, they write the process, steps, materials and ingredients (approx. 
measurements) used in making their dish. This helps them understand the process 
involved. Each group is then asked to find the exact number of serving size, quantity of 
©Anju Musaﬁr-Chazot, Anita Shah & Komal Saksena, Mahatma Gandhi Interna/onal School, Ahmedabad. !6
documents.subject: Social Science

documents.text:
each ingredient that will be required and the cost of each ingredient. This will help us get 
the cost price of each serving. Once they have achieved this, they will find out of the 
selling price of the dish. 
• Students go to a local market to buy the ingredients and also explore different brands 
and quality of products by reading food labels. 
04 Immediate reflection 
• They reflect on the type of recipe, quantity, pricing etc. They also reflect on their trip to 
the market and on the availability, pricing of products. How ecological is their 
sourcing? Is the ingredient local? How much of waste is generated by disposing the 
packaging if it is packed? Or can it be reused? Can they reduce the costs by switching 
the ingredients or source? 
05 Creation (Mind map, posters) 
• They create a mind/concept map of running a café in school. individually, This can be 
done in pairs or in groups of 4. They create a common mind map and share with other 
groups.  
• As a class a new mind map is created using each groups idea.  
• Now, the students assign different roles and responsibilities needed for the café such as 
chef, cleaners, servers, accounts team, managers, marketing team, etc. they vote and 
choose the role they want to try.  
• Students create posters individually giving their café a name, logo and drawing their 
dishes artistically. Students present their poster and feedback is given for each poster using 
criteria defined by them. 
• The best name and poster is chosen by the class and used for the final café. The others 
are displayed in class. 
• The students run the café with each sub-group handling different domains such as 
cooking, serving, maintaining accounts, looking after clients etc.  After that they calculate 
the proﬁt or loss from selling their dishes.
06 Feedback
• Students seek and give feedback related to their own role, the dish prepared, how it 
was received by their ‘client group’ etc. 
©Anju Musaﬁr-Chazot, Anita Shah & Komal Saksena, Mahatma Gandhi Interna/onal School, Ahmedabad. !7
documents.subject: Social Science

documents.text:
07 Reﬂection
• Students make connections in their understanding of different roles, their duties and the 
collaboration required amongst them. They reﬂect on what worked well, what was 
challenging, what needs to be improved. They also think about food habits, hygiene, 
health and whether their costing, quantity was appropriate. They reﬂect on how they 
can do things differently the next time. Most importantly, what did they feel? Which 
part or role did they enjoy the most? Cooking? Or serving? Or managing the accounts? 
What are the important skills they have learnt? Which new role would they like to take 
up for the next session for running the café and making a new dish?
08 Feedback
• They share what they have learnt through all these activities, how it relates to their life 
and whether they feel it has shifted anything in their beliefs or understanding about 
food and health.  They can share the most important skill they feel they have learnt 
through this module.
©Anju Musaﬁr-Chazot, Anita Shah & Komal Saksena, Mahatma Gandhi Interna/onal School, Ahmedabad. !8

Transaction would proceed in the following manner- 
Active Learning- Frayer Model on thermometer. (Critical Thinking) 
 
Group Learning- The class will be divided into eight groups. Jigsaw 
Expert Group: The group will be given worksheet on three modes of 
transfer of heat  
Learning Group: Students will teach each other the different modes of 
transfer of heat. (Communication, Collaboration) 
  
Differentiation- The students in groups of 8 will be demonstrating the 
transfer of heat in solids and liquids. (Character, Communication) 
 
Questioning- Multiple level question- Teacher will prepare a list of 
question about conduction, convection and radiation and will ask these 
questions after discussion. (Critical Thinking, Communication) 
 
Brain Storming-The class would start with a discussion on what the 
students have already learnt in the previous classes and hence what is it that 
they would learn now. They would also be told the significance of the topic 
that they would be studying. 
 
Introduction of the topic- PPT and Digital Content would be shared. 
 
Facilitation of content 
The facilitator will enable the learners to understand the fundamental 
concept of Heat. 
He/ She will compare and contrast different modes of transfer of heat. 
 
Approaches 
The facilitator should apply some or all the approaches while administering 
the teaching learning process. 
 Didactic Approach 
 Summarizing Approach 
 Feedback Approach 
 
Techniques to be used: 
 Quiz 
 MCQ 
 PPT

(4) Synthetic indicator-phenolphthalein :

Phenolphthalein is another commonly used indicator. Its solution is colorless
and remains colorless in acidic and neutral solution but, it gives pink color in
basic solution. Therefore it in considered as base indicator.

Neutralization :

The reaction between an acid and a base is known as neutralization
reaction. Salt and water are produced in this process with evolution of heat.
In neutraliation reaction, new substance is formed. This is called salt. Salt
may be acdic, basic or neutral in nature. Thus neutralisation reaction can be
defined as

Acid + Base-------- — Salt +Water +Heat
e.g. HCl + NaOH — NaCl + H,O + Heat

Activity 2 : To understand the process of neutralization.

Material Required : Beakers, test tubes, dilute hydrchloric acid,
Phenolphthalein, Sodium hydroxide, dropper etc.

Method: Take 2-3 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid in a test tube. Add 2-3
drops of phenolphthalein solution. No colour is formed because phenolphthalein
remain colorless in acidic and neutral solutions. Now take sodium hydroxide
solution in another test tube and add 2-3 drops of phenolphthalein. The
formation of pink colour indicates the basic nature of sodium hydroxide.Now
add few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid to it.

Observation : The pink colour of the solution disappears.

Conclusion: Above activity shows that adding suitable amount of a base
to acidic solution, makes it neutral.

Acid + Base > Salt + Water + Heat

documents.text:
51
Breaking stereotypes
Engine drivers are men. But 27-year-old Laxmi Lakra, from a
poor tribal family in Jharkhand has begun to change things.
She is the first woman engine driver for Northern Railways.
Laxmi·s parents are not literate but they struggled and
overcame many hardships to make sure their children got an
education. Laxmi studied in a government school. Even in school,
Laxmi helped with the housework and did odd jobs. She studied
hard and did well and then went on to get a diploma in
electronics. She then took the railway board exam and passed
it on her first attempt.
Laxmi says, ´I love challenges and the moment somebody says it
is not for girls, I make sure I go ahead and do it.µ  Laxmi has had
to do this several times in her life ² when she wanted to take electronics; when she rode
motorcycles at the polytechnic; and when she decided to become an engine driver.
Her philosophy is simple ² ´As long as I am having fun without harming anyone, as long as I am
doing well and helping my parents,  why should I not lead a lifestyle of my choice?µ
(Adapted from Driving Her Train by Neeta Lal, Women·s Features Service)
Fewer opportunities and rigid expectations
A lot of the children in Rosie Ma·am·s class drew
women as nurses and men as army officers. The
reason they did this is because they feel that outside
the home too, women are good at only certain jobs.
For example, many people believe that women make
better nurses because they are more patient and
gentle. This is linked to women·s roles within the
family. Similarly, it is believed that science requires
a technical mind and girls and women are not capable
of dealing with technical things.
Because so many people believe in these
stereotypes, many girls do not get the same support
that boys do to study and train to become doctors
and engineers. In most families, once girls finish
school, they are encouraged by their families to see
marriage as their main aim in life.

Social and Political Life
Read the story below and answer
the questions ²
If you were Xavier, what subject
would you choose and why?
In your experience, what are some
of the other pressures that boys
experience?
Xavier was happy with the results of his Class X
board exams. Though his marks in Science and
Maths were not high, he had done well in his
favourite subjects ² History and Languages.  When
his parents saw his report card, however, they did
not look pleased at all...
My Goodness! Xavier,  you have
managed only 65% in Maths. Your marks
in Physics are low too...
I know Mama, but it·s
okay, because I don·t
want to take Maths or
Science. I want to
study History.
   Why do you want to take History?
Think about your future.
You have to get a good job!
    History will not help. It has no scope!
But, but, I don·t like
Maths or Science!
Be sensible, son. Take Maths, and you can
study computers side by side. The job market
for computers is very good.
It is important to understand that we live in a
society in which all children face pressures from the
world around them. Sometimes, these come in the
form of demands from adults. At other times, they
can just be because of unfair teasing by our own
friends. Boys are pressurised to think about getting
a job that will pay a good salary. They are also teased
and bullied if they do not behave like other boys.
You may remember that in your Class VI book you
read about how boys at an early age are encouraged
not to cry in front of others.

53
Ramabai (1858ĩ1922), shown above
with her daughter, championed the cause
of womenĬs education. She never went to
school but learnt to read and write from
her parents. She was given the title
īPanditaĬ because she could read and
write Sanskrit, a remarkable
achievement as women then were not
allowed such knowledge. She went on to
set up a Mission in Khedgaon near Pune
in 1898, where widows and poor women
were encouraged not only to become
literate but to be independent. They were
taught a variety of skills from carpentry
to running a printing press, skills that
are not usually taught to girls even today.
The printing press can be seen in the
picture on the top left corner. RamabaiĬs
Mission is still active today.
Learning for change
Going to school is an extremely important part of
your life. As more and more children enter school
every year, we begin to think that it is normal for all
children to go to school. Today, it is difficult for us
to imagine that school and learning could be seen
as ´out of boundsµ or not appropriate for some
children. But in the past, the skill of reading and
writing was known to only a few. Most children learnt
the work their families or elders did. For girls, the
situation was worse. In communities that taught sons
to read and write, daughters were not allowed to learn
the alphabet. Even in families where skills like
pottery, weaving and craft were taught, the
contribution of daughters and women was only seen
as supportive. For example, in the pottery trade,
women collected the mud and prepared the earth
for the pots. But since they did not operate the wheel,
they were not seen as potters.
In the nineteenth century, many new ideas about
education and learning emerged. Schools became
more common and communities that had never
learnt reading and writing started sending their
children to school. But there was a lot of opposition
to educating girls even then. Yet many women and
men made efforts to open schools for girls. Women
struggled to learn to read and write.

Social and Political Life
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain and her dreams about ¶Ladyland·
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain (1880 ²1932) was born into a rich family who owned a lot of land.  Though
she knew how to read and write Urdu, she was stopped from learning Bangla and English. In those
days, English was seen as a language that would expose girls to new ideas, which people thought were
not correct for them. Therefore, it was mostly boys who were taught English. Rokeya learnt
to read and write Bangla and English with the support of her elder brother and an elder
sister.  She went on to become a writer. She wrote a remarkable story titled
Sultana·s Dream in 1905 to practise her English skills when she was merely 25
years old. This story imagined a woman called Sultana who reaches a place
called Ladyland. Ladyland is a place where women had the freedom to study,
work, and create inventions like controlling rain from the clouds and
flying air cars. In this Ladyland, the men had been sent into seclusion ²
their aggressive guns and other weapons of war defeated by the brain-
power of women. As Sultana travels in Ladyland with Sister Sarah,
she awakes to realise that she was only dreaming.
As you can see, Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain was dreaming of
women flying planes and cars even before girls were being
allowed to go to school! This was the way in which education
and learning had changed Rokeya·s own life.  Rokeya did not
stop at getting education just for herself. Her education gave
her the power not only to dream and write, but also to do
more ² to help other girls go to school and to build their
own dreams.  In 1910, she started a school for girls in Kolkata,
and to this day, the school is still functioning.
Learning to read and write led some
women to question the situation of
women in society. They wrote stories,
letters and autobiographies describing
their own experiences of inequality. In
their writings, they also imagined new
ways of thinking and living for both
men and women.
Let us read about the experience of Rashsundari
Devi (1800²1890), who was born in West Bengal,
some 200 years ago. At the age of 60, she wrote her
autobiography in Bangla. Her book titled Amar Jiban
is the first known autobiography written by an Indian
woman. Rashsundari Devi was a housewife from a
rich landlord·s family. At that time, it was believed
that if a woman learnt to read and write, she would
bring bad luck to her husband and become a widow!
Despite this, she taught herself how to read and write
in secret, well after her marriage.
´I would start working at dawn, and I would still
be at it until well beyond midnight. I had no rest in
between. I was only fourteen years old at the time. I
came to nurture a great longing: I would learn to
read and I would read a religious manuscript. I was

Unlike Rashsundari Devi and Rokeya
Hossain, who were not allowed to learn
to read and write, large numbers of girls
attend school in India today. Despite this,
there continue to be many girls who leave
school for reasons of poverty, inadequate
schooling facilities and discrimination.
Providing equal schooling facilities to
children from all communities and class
backgrounds, and particularly girls,
continues to be a challenge in India.
unlucky, in those days women were not educated.
Later, I began to resent my own thoughts. What is
wrong with me? Women do not read, how will I do
it? Then I had a dream: I was reading the manuscript
of Chaitanya Bhagabat (the life of a saint)« Later in
the day, as I sat cooking in the kitchen, I heard my
husband say to my eldest son: ´Bepin, I have left my
Chaitanya Bhagabat here. When I ask for it, bring it
in.µ He left the book there and went away. When the
book had been taken inside, I secretly took out a
page and hid it carefully. It was a job hiding it, for
nobody must find it in my hands. My eldest son was
practising his alphabets at that time. I hid one of
them as well. At times, I went over that, trying to
match letters from that page with the letters that I
remembered. I also tried to match the words with
those that I would hear in the course of my days.
With tremendous care and effort, and over a long
period of time, I learnt how to read«µ
After learning the alphabet, Rashsundari Devi was
able to read the Chaitanya Bhagabat. Through her
own writing she also gave the world an opportunity
to read about women·s lives in those days.
Rashsundari Devi wrote about her everyday life
experiences in details. There were days when she
did not have a moment·s rest, no time even to sit
down and eat!
Schooling and education today
Today, both boys and girls attend school in large
numbers. Yet, as we will see, there still remain
differences between the education of boys and girls.
India has a census every 10 years, which counts the
whole population of the country. It also gathers
detailed information about the people living in
India ² their age, schooling, what work they do, and
so on. We use this information to measure many
things, like the number of literate people, and the
ratio of men and women. According to the 1961
census, about 40 per cent of all boys and men

Women·s movement
Women and girls now have the right to study and go
to school. There are other spheres ² like legal reform,
violence and health ² where the situation of women
and girls has improved. These changes have not
happened automatically. Women individually, and
collectively have struggled to bring about these
changes. This struggle is known as the Women·s
Movement. Individual women and women·s
organisations from different parts of the country are
part of the movement. Many men support the women·s
movement as well. The diversity, passion and efforts
of those involved makes it a very vibrant movement.
Different strategies have been used to spread
awareness, fight discrimination and seek justice.
Here are some glimpses of this struggle.

Campaigning
Campaigns to fight discrimination
and violence against women are an
important part of the women·s
movement. Campaigns have also led
to new laws being passed. A law was
made in 2006 to give women who face
physical and mental violence within
their homes, also called domestic
violence, some legal protection.
Similarly, efforts made by the
women·s movement led the Supreme
Court to formulate guidelines in 1997
to protect women against sexual
harassment at the workplace and
within educational institutions.
In the 1980s, for example, women·s
groups across the country spoke out
against ¶dowry deaths· ³ cases of
young brides being murdered by their
in-laws or husbands, greedy for more
dowry. Women·s groups spoke out
against the failure to bring these
cases to justice. They did so by
coming on to the streets, approaching
the courts, and by sharing
information. Eventually, this became
a public issue in the newspapers and
society, and the dowry laws were
changed to punish families who seek
dowry.
Satyarani, an active member of the womenĬs movement,
sitting on the steps of the Supreme Court surrounded by legal
files gathered during the course of a long legal battle to seek
justice for her daughter who was murdered for dowry.
documents.subject: Social Science

documents.text:
Raising Awareness
An important part of the women·s
movements· work is to raise public
awareness on women·s rights issues.
Their message has been spread through
street plays, songs and public meetings.
Protesting
The women·s movement raises its voice when violations against women take place or
for example, when a law or policy acts against their interests. Public rallies and
demonstrations are a very powerful way of drawing attention to injustices.

Showing Solidarity
The women·s movement is also about showing
solidarity with other women and causes.
Above: Women are holding up
candles to demonstrate the
solidarity between the people of
India and Pakistan. Every year, on
14 August, several thousand people
gather at Wagah on the border of
India and Pakistan and hold a
cultural programme.
Below: On 8 March, International WomenĬs Day, women all over
the world come together to celebrate and renew their struggles.

Glossary
Stereotype: When we believe that people belonging to particular groups based on religion, wealth,
language are bound to have certain fixed characteristics or can only do a certain type of work, we
create a stereotype. For example, in this chapter, we saw how boys and girls are made to take
certain subjects not because he or she has an aptitude for it, but because they are either boys or
girls. Stereotypes prevent us from looking at people as unique individuals.
Discrimination: When we do not treat people equally or with respect we are indulging in
discrimination. It happens when people or organisations act on their prejudices. Discrimination
usually takes place when we treat some one differently or make a distinction.
Violation: When someone forcefully breaks the law or a rule or openly shows disrespect, we can
say that he or she has committed a violation.
Sexual harassment: This refers to physical or verbal behaviour that is of a sexual nature and
against the wishes of a woman.

documents.text:
Media
Teacher·s note
Today, the media and advertising are a
pervasive presence in the lives of young
people, who may or may not have taken
the opportunity to seriously reflect upon
this fact. This Unit offers some ways by
which we can begin to think about these.
The focus is on explaining the strong
links between media and technology and
media and big business.  It explains how
the media ¶sets the agenda· through
influencing our perception of issues
worth devoting time and attention to,
and issues that are neglected or
overridden.
Chapter 6 foregrounds the widespread
effects of the media, and attempts to
connect the issues under discussion to the
learner·s own lives.  At the end of the
chapter, we expect the learner to recognise
the role of big business in the media
coverage of events ³ the way ¶news· is
selected for coverage, and the explicit/
implicit dimensions of that coverage. We
use two fictitious news reports to
demonstrate that there is seldom just one
version of a story or an event.  Building on
this, we expect the learner to develop the
skills required to critically analyse a
newspaper report or a TV story through
scrutinising the information provided, as
well as understanding the logic behind the
exclusion of certain perspectives.
These ideas can be strengthened by
selecting 
examples 
from 
actual
advertisements and structuring similar
questions around them.
This chapter concludes by linking its
contents to the idea of democracy.  It
emphasises, through using examples of
local media as well as social advertising,
how mainstream media and advertising
tend to favour those who have greater
financial as well as social resources. This
point can be reinforced in the classroom
by using local examples of media stories,
as well as posing questions about the ways
in which advertising is changing what is
locally available as well as locally valued.

LET'S TRY TO ANSWER THIS QUESTION
Q. A substance present in food that is used by the body to support normal growth, maintenance,
and repair is called a nutrient. Is water a nutrient?
Yes, because it is one of the sources of energy.
No, because it is not present in all the food items.
Yes, because it is essential to keep the body in good health.
No, because it is thrown out of our body along with the waste.
How did students perform?
What is the mistake?
Students are not able to identify the role of
water as a nutrient.
LET'S UNDERSTAND WHERE THE MISTAKE IS HAPPENING...
The question tests whether the student understands the importance of water as a nutrient.
42.6% of the students have opted for the correct answer option C. This shows that the
students understand the role played by water in maintaining hydration, metabolism, ion
balance in the body, transportation of waste, etc which result in normal growth, maintenance,
and repair. 29.9% of the students opted for the wrong answer option D. This may be because
students may have a misconception that we drink water to only satisfy our thirst and later the
water is removed from the body through micturition. 14.3% of the students have opted for the
wrong answer option A. This shows that the students have a misconception that minerals
provide energy to the body. 9.8% of the students have opted for the wrong answer option B.
This may be because the students have an incomplete understanding of the water content in
the food items they eat.  
LET'S CORRECT THIS MISTAKE
It is important for the students to understand the
importance of water in the healthy functioning of
their bodies. To remediate the misconception,
teachers may help students by asking them to make a
table of food the students eat every day. The teacher
can further help students by breaking down each
food item in the list in terms of nutrients they
provide like water, minerals, protein, vitamins,
carbohydrates, etc. Put a tick mark in the table for
the nutrient found in each food. This will help
students to know the importance of water and other
minerals.

SCIENCE

4

e use in our daily life a large
number of substances such
as lemon, tamarind, common
salt, sugar and vinegar. Do they have
the same taste? Let us recall tastes of
some edible substances listed in
Table 4.1. If you have not tasted any of
these substances taste it now and enter
the result in Table 4.1.
You find that some of these
substances taste sour, some taste bitter,
some taste sweet and some taste salty.
4.1 ACIDS AND BASES
Curd, lemon juice, orange juice and
vinegar taste sour. These substances
taste sour because they contain acids.
The chemical nature of such substances
is acidic. The word acid comes from the
Latin word acere which means sour.
The acids in these substances are
natural acids.
What about baking soda? Does it also
taste sour? If not, what is its taste? Since,
it does not taste sour it means, that it
has no acids in it. It is bitter in taste. If
you rub its solution between fingers, it
feels soapy. Generally, substances like
these which are bitter in taste and feel
soapy on touching are known as bases.
The nature of such substances is said to
be basic.
If we cannot taste every substance,
how do we find its nature?
Special type of substances are used
to test whether a substance is acidic or
basic. These substances are known as
indicators. The indicators change their
colour when added to a solution
containing an acidic or a basic
substance. Turmeric, litmus, China rose
petals (Gudhal), etc., are some of the
naturally occurring indicators.
CAUTION
1. Do not taste anything unless asked
to do so.
2. Do not touch anything unless asked
to do so.

4.3 NEUTRALISATION
We have learnt that acids turn blue
litmus red and bases turn red litmus
blue. Let us see what happens when an
acid is mixed with a base.
We are going to use an indicator you

Are you familiar with the term acid rain? Have you ever heard about damaging
effect of acid rain? As the name indicates the rain containing excess of acids is
called an acid rain. Where do these acids come from? The rain becomes acidic
because carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide (which are released
into the air as pollutants) dissolve in rain drops to form carbonic acid, sulphuric
acid and nitric acid respectively. Acid rain can cause damage to buildings,
historical monuments, plants and animals.

documents.text:
SCIENCE
88
 When an acidic solution is mixed
with a basic solution, both the solutions
neutralise the effect of each other. When
an acid solution and a base solution are
mixed in suitable amounts, both the
acidic nature of the acid and the basic
nature of the base are destroyed. The
resulting solution is neither acidic nor
basic. Touch the test tube immediately
after neutralisation. What do you
observe? In neutralisation reaction, heat
is always produced, or evolved. The
evolved heat raises the temperature of
the reaction mixture.
In neutralisation reaction a new
substance is formed. This is called salt.
Salt may be acidic, basic or neutral in
nature. Thus, neutralisation can be
defined as follows:
The reaction between an acid and
a base is known as neutralisation. Salt
and water are produced in this process
with the evolution of heat.
Acid+Base  Salt+Water
     (Heat is evolved)
The following reaction is an example:
Hydrochloric acid (HCl) + Sodium
hydroxide (NaOH) 
Sodium chloride (NaCl) + Water (H2O)
Boojho added dilute sulphuric acid
to lime water. Will the reaction mixture
become hot or cool?
4.4 NEUTRALISATION IN EVERYDAY
LIFE
Indigestion
Our stomach contains hydrochloric
acid. It helps us to digest food, as you
have learnt in Chapter 2. But too
much of acid in the stomach causes
indigestion. Sometimes indigestion
is painful. To relieve indigestion, we
take an antacid such as milk of
magnesia, which contains magnesium
hydroxide. It neutralises the effect of
excessive acid.
Ant bite
When an ant bites, it injects
the acidic liquid (formic acid) into the
skin. The effect of the acid can be
neutralised by rubbing moist baking
soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) or
calamine solution, which contains zinc
carbonate.
Soil treatment
Excessive use of chemical fertilisers
makes the soil acidic. Plants do not
grow well when the soil is either too
acidic or too basic. When the soil is
too acidic, it is treated with bases like
quick lime (calcium oxide) or slaked
lime (calcium hydroxide). If the soil
is basic, organic matter (compost) is
added to it. Organic matter releases
acids which neutralises the basic
nature of the soil.
Factory wastes
The wastes of many factories
contain acids. If they are allowed to
flow into the water bodies, the acids
will kill fish and other organisms.
The factory wastes are, therefore,
neutralised 
by 
adding 
basic
substances.

SCIENCE
90
What you have learnt

Acids are sour in taste. Generally, bases are bitter in taste and soapy
to touch.

Acid turns blue litmus red. Bases turn red litmus blue.

Substances which are neither acidic nor basic are called neutral.

Solutions of substances that show different colour in acidic, basic and
neutral solutions are called indicators.

An acid and a base neutralise each other and form a salt. A salt may be
acidic, basic or neutral in nature.
Exercises
1.
State differences between acids and bases.
2.
Ammonia is found in many household products, such as window
cleaners. It turns red litmus blue. What is its nature?
3.
Name the source from which litmus solution is obtained. What is the
use of this solution?
4.
Is the distilled water acidic/basic/neutral? How would you verify it?
5.
Describe the process of neutralisation with the help of an example.
6.
Mark ‘T’ if the statement is true and ‘F’ if it is false:
(i)
Nitric acid turn red litmus blue. (T/F)
(ii)
Sodium hydroxide turns blue litmus red. (T/F)
(iii)
Sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid neutralise each other and
form salt and water. (T/F)
(iv)
Indicator is a substance which shows different colours in acidic
and basic solutions. (T/F)
(v)
Tooth decay is caused by the presence of a base. (T/F)
7.
Dorji has a few bottles of soft drink in his restaurant. But, unfortu-
nately, these are not labelled. He has to serve the drinks on the demand
of customers. One customer wants acidic drink, another wants basic
and third one wants neutral drink. How will Dorji decide which drink is
to be served to whom?
8.
Explain why:
(a)
An antacid tablet is taken when you suffer from acidity.

Did you know?
Each cell in our body contains an acid, the deoxyribonucleic acid or
DNA. It controls every feature of the body such as our looks, colour of

Theorem and proof

How do we conclude that the sum of the angles
in any triangle is 180°? Is it enough if we draw
several triangles, measure the angles and
check the sum? How can we say for sure that
for a triangle not among these, the sum is 180°?

In any triangle, we can draw a line through
one vertex, parallel to the opposite side. And
then using the relations between angles made
by parallel lines, we can see that the sum of
the angles of a triangle is 180°.

By doing this, we achieve much.

° Even if we change the triangle, the
arguments used do not change. So, the
conclusion of these arguments also is
true for the changed triangle.

° Properties of parallel lines can be easily
recognized. But the fact that sum of the
angles of a triangle is 180°, is not
immediately obvious. This is an example
of establishing complex ideas, starting
from simple truths.

° When arguments are linked one after
another using ideas of parallel lines, we
not only get the theorem that sum of
the angles of a triangle is 180°, but also
see why it is so.

Measures and relations

We can draw squares of different sizes. The
perimeter and area change with the length of
sides. But in all the squares, the perimeter is
always four times the length of side; and the
area is the product of the length of side by
itself.

There are many such situations where even
though the measures change, certain relations
between them do not change. For example, if
we take several objects made of iron, their
volume and weight will be different. But if
we divide the weight by the volume, we get
the same number, 7.8. This is called the density
of iron. Similarly if we do this for objects made
of copper, weight divided by volume gives 8.9.
This is the density of copper.

In such contexts, the unchanging relation
between measures is denoted using letters.
For example, if we write the weight ofan object
made of iron as w and the volume as v, then
we can write

w= 7.8v

If we take copper instead of iron, the relation
will be

w = 8.9v

In general, if the weight of an object is w, its
volume is v and if it is made of a material of
density d, then their relation can be written as

w=dv

Look at these sums:
1+2 = 3
2+3 = 5
3+4=7

We add two consecutive natural numbers.

Now look at these:
(2x1) +1 = 3
(2x2) +1 = 5
(2x3) +1=7

We double natural numbers and add 1.
How come we end up with the same numbers?

Let's take a natural number and do the first operation. For
example, if we start with 7, the next natural number is 8;
and the sum

7+8=15
Suppose we write the 8 here as 7 + 1? We see that

T+74+1=(2x7T)+1=15

This we can do for any natural number instead of 7.

Can we do this only with natural numbers?
For example let's take the fraction, half: There is no meaning
in saying the next fraction; but we can say, the number got

by adding one to it. That is, half and one make one and a
half. The half we started with, together with the one and a
half we got now makes two.

On the other hand, doubling half makes one; and one added
to it makes 2. That is,

Measures and numbers

Numbers were invented by Man to indicate
and compare various measurements. For
example, instead of saying, “a large group of
people”, if we say, “a group of hundred
people”, one gets a clear picture. Or instead
of saying “walked some distance”, we can be
more precise and say, “walked two and a half
kilometers”.

Length, weight and time are measured directly
using instruments; area, volume and density
are not directly measured, but are got by
computations. For that we need operations
with numbers. For example, to find volume of
a rectangular block we must measure its
length, width and height and calculate the
product.

In course of time, men started thinking about
operations with pure numbers without linking
them to measurement. For example, after
discovering that

to compute the perimeter of a rectangle,
instead of measuring all four sides and
adding, we need only measure two
different sides and then double their sum

they went on to discover the number principle
that

instead of multiplying two numbers
separately by two and adding, we need only
multiply their sum by two.

Much latter, we started writing this using letters
as

What happens when we add the sum and

Difference is the smaller number subtracted

Look at this problem:

If we forget about books and pens and look at
the prices as mere numbers, the problem is
like this:

The sum of two numbers is 16 and their
difference is 10. What are the numbers?

Double the larger number is 16 + 10 = 26; so
the larger number is 13. And then the smaller
number is 16 — 13 = 3. Thus the price of the
book is 13 rupees and the price of the pen is 3
rupees.

There is another way. Instead of a book and
pen, suppose two books are bought. Since the
price of the book is 10 rupees more, we would
have to give 10 more rupees; that is, 16 + 10 =
26 rupees.

This is the price of two books. So, the price of
one book is 13 rupees.

100 one-rupee coins are to be put into several
pouches, such that any amount upto 100 rupees

Another problem: Raju has 200 rupees with him and Rahim

girls and 20 boys. What is the ratio of the number of girls

to the number of boys?

If we split the girls and boys separately into groups of 5,
there will be 5 groups of girls and 4 groups of boys. So the

ratio is 5 to 4.

Number properties

We need algebra to show that certain proper-
ties are true for all numbers. For example, to
prove that the sum of any two consecutive
natural numbers is an odd number, we must
first note that if a natural number is denoted
by n, then the next natural number is n+ 1

show that whatever be the natural number 7,
the number 27 + 1 is an odd number.

In many other sciences, if a certain fact is veri-
fied in a number of different contexts, then it
is accepted as a general principle. This is not
enough in mathematics. We must also show
why it must be true in all cases. For numbers
such reasoning is explained using algebra.

There are several instances where some facts
are true for several numbers and then fail. For
example if we divide 2? by 2, 2° by 3, 2* by 4

Some history

Abu al-Wafa was a famous mathematician and
astronomer who lived in Baghdad during the
tenth century AD.

One of his books is "On Those Parts of
Geometry Needed by Craftsmen." In it, he
discusses various methods of joining small
squares to make large squares and cutting large
squares to make smaller squares.

One such discussion demonstrates that the
method used by the craftsmen then to join three
squares into one is not accurate and also gives
the correct method. It is this method that is
given under Three squares in this lesson.

  Congruence of Segments 
Activity I 	 Take a rectangular paper. Place two 
	
	
	
opposite sides one upon the other. 
	
	
	
They coincide exactly.
Activity II 	 Using the ruler measure the lengths 
	
	
	
of seg AB and seg PQ.
	
	
	
l(AB) = .............	
l(PQ) = .............
	
Are they of the same length? You cannot pick up and place one segment over the 
other. Trace the seg AB along with the names of the points on a sheet of transparent paper. 
Place this new segment on seg PQ. Verify that if point A is placed on point P, then B falls 
on Q. It means that seg AB is congruent with seg PQ. 
	
We can infer from this that if two line segments have the same lengths, they coincide 
exactly with each other. That is, they are congruent. If seg AB and seg PQ are 
congruent, it is written as seg AB ≅ seg PQ.
Now I know !
If given line segments are equal in length, they are congruent.
{ 
If seg AB ≅ seg PQ it means that seg PQ ≅ seg AB.

   Co-prime numbers : Two numbers which have only 1 as a common factor are said 
to be co-prime or relatively prime or mutually prime numbers.
	
For example, 10 and 21 are co-primes, because the divisors of 10 are 1, 2, 5, 10

We got two different answers because the two children carried out the operations 
in different orders. To prevent this, some rules have been made which decide the order 
in which the operations are carried out. If these rules are followed, we will always 
get the same answer. When an operation is to be carried out first, it is shown using 
brackets in the expression.
Rules for Simplifying an Expression
(1)	 If more than one operation is to be carried out, then multiplication and division 
are carried out first, in the order in which they occur from left to right.
(2)	 After that, addition and subtraction are carried out in the order in which they occur 
from left to right.
(3)	 If there are more than one operations in the brackets, follow the above two rules 
while carrying out the operations.

Example  The length of a rectangle is 1 cm more 
than twice its breadth. If the perimeter of the 
rectangle is 50 cm, find its length.
Solution:  
Let the breadth of the rectangle be x cm. 
Then the length of the rectangle will be (2x +1)cm.
2 × length + 2 × breadth = perimeter of rectangle
	
		
	
 2 (2x + 1) + 2x = 50
	
		
	
∴  4x + 2 + 2x 	= 50
	
		
	
        ∴ 6x + 2 = 50
	
		
	
             ∴ 6x = 50 - 2 = 48
	
		
	
              ∴  x = 8
Breadth of rectangle is 8 cm.
Length of the rectangle = 2x + 1 = 2 × 8 + 1 
∴	 Length of rectangle = 17 cm.

Inverse Proportion
	
Some volunteers have gathered to dig 90 pits for 
a tree plantation programme. One volunteer digs one 
pit in one day. If there are 15 volunteers, they will 
take 
90
15  = 6 days to dig the pits. 
10 volunteers will take 
90
10  = 9 days.
Are the number of pits and the number of volunteers 
in direct proportion?
	
If the number of volunteers decreases, more days are required; and if the number 
of volunteers increases, fewer days are required for the job. However, the product 
of the number of days and number of volunteers remains constant. We say that 
these numbers are in inverse proportion. 
·	 Suppose  Sudha  has  to  solve  48  problems  in a problem set. If she solves 
1 problem every day, she will need 48 days to complete the set. But, if she solves 
8 problems every day, she will complete the set in 48
8  = 6 days and if she solves 
12 problems a day, she will need 
48
12  = 4 days. The number of problems solved 
in a day and the number of days needed are in inverse proportion. Their product 
is constant. 
	
	
Thus, note that 8 × 6 = 12 × 4 = 48 × 1
