Period 10:   Speaking 
LO:  Students will be able to demonstrate speaking skills by asking questions politely 
and gathering information in a respectful manner. 
Hook: 
The teacher asks the following questions:
documents.subject: English

documents.text:
220 
● First, ask in a rude or abrupt way (e.g., "What’s your name?" with no tone of respect). 
● Then, rephrase the same question politely (e.g., "Could you please tell me your 
name?"). 
(NOTE: Pause after each version to gauge reactions and make a point about how tone 
and wording affect the conversation.) 
● Which version felt more comfortable to answer? Why do you think that is? 
Experience and Reflection: 
Imagine you’re meeting a new friend at school. How would you introduce yourself 
and ask them questions? 
 
Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do)                    
Today, we're going to learn how to ask questions politely and listen carefully when we 
meet new people.  
The teacher facilities a discussion using the questions below: 
Imagine you're meeting someone for the first time— 
● How do you think you should talk to them to make a good impression? 
● When you meet a new friend, what’s the first thing you say? How do you introduce 
yourself? 
● What are some questions to ask someone to know about them? (e.g. favourite things, 
like their favourite colour or food,etc.) 
The teacher demonstrates role-play using some questions from the textbook. 
Let’s practice! I’ll pretend to be a new student, and you can ask me questions. Make sure to 
ask politely and listen carefully to my answers 
 
CFU (Open-ended/ Factual) 
Factual 
1. Do you think asking questions politely and listening carefully will help you make new friends 
at school? Why or why not?          
Open-ended 
1.Why is it important to listen carefully when someone answers your question? 
 
 
Group Work (We Do)
documents.subject: English

documents.text:
221 
The teacher divides the class into pairs. One student will be the "detective," and the other will 
be the "interviewee." The detective asks the questions listed on page 96 in the "Speaking" 
section of the textbook, while the interviewee responds comfortably. After the interview, 
students will switch roles, allowing both to practice asking and answering questions. 
(Note for Students: You can also add a few questions of your choice) 
 
Independent Work (You Do)                        
After role-play the teacher asks students to reflect on the following questions: 
1. What did you learn about your partner? 
2. How did asking polite questions make the conversation? 
3. How did you feel when you were asking questions? 
4. Did you find it hard to answer any of the questions? Why? 
 
Closing                                                                                   
Today, we learnt how asking questions politely and listening carefully helps us communicate 
better and build connections. 
 
Home Work 
Use polite questioning and active listening when talking to a family member or a friend. Write 
a reflection on how the conversation goes and how it felt to ask and listen carefully. 
For example: Conversation with a family member about a recent event, conversation with a 
friend about their favourite hobby, etc. 
 
Assessment (Think of what children SAY, DO and MAKE while learning that can form the 
evidence of learning to be used for assessment) 
Answer the following questions:  
1. Write three polite questions you could ask a new friend at school. 
2. Think about a time when you met a new person, like a new student or neighbour. How did 
asking polite questions and listening carefully help you get to know them better? What made 
the conversation enjoyable? Write your answer below. 
Assessment can also be conducted using the following observations: 
• Observe students during the activity to ensure they are asking questions politely and 
listening attentively.
documents.subject: English

documents.text:
222 
• "Did the student ask their questions in a respectful way?" 
• "Was the student paying attention and responding to others?" 
• Evaluate their ability to engage in meaningful conversations, ask follow-up questions, 
and express themselves clearly. 
• "Did the student ask questions that helped the conversation move forward?" 
• "Did the student speak clearly and explain their ideas well?" 
• Provide individual feedback at the end of the lesson based on participation and 
communication skills. 
• "How did the student contribute to the discussion?" 
• "What can the student do to improve their communication next time?" 
 
Period 11:  Writing 
LO: Students will be able to demonstrate writing well-organized paragraphs with clear topic 
sentences and supporting details. 
Hook: Imagine you meet someone who never speaks to anyone, lives alone, and seems like a 
mystery. What would you think about them? Would you be curious to know more, or would you 
just walk away? 
Experience and Reflection: 
Have you ever met someone who seemed quiet or different from others? How did you feel about 
them, and did you ever try to understand their story? 
 
Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do)                     
The teacher displays a sample paragraph and guides a discussion on the basic structure of a 
paragraph. The teacher will highlight how each part of the paragraph supports the main idea 
about Mr. Nath. 
 
Example: "Mr. Nath is a mysterious man who lives alone. He is often seen by the children but 
does not interact with them much. His quiet nature makes him seem unapproachable, yet there 
are rumours that he might be hiding something." 
Topic Sentence: "Mr. Nath is a mysterious man who lives alone." 
Supporting Details: "He is often seen by the children but does not interact with them much. His 
quiet nature makes him seem unapproachable." 
Concluding Statement: "Yet there are rumours that he might be hiding something.
documents.subject: English

documents.text:
223 
Group Work (We Do)                                 
Divide the class into pairs and have students work together to brainstorm answers to the two 
questions about Mr. Nath. Each pair will then write two paragraphs: 
1. A paragraph about who Mr. Nath is, including at least three supporting details from the text 
to describe his character. 
2. A paragraph continues the story, predicting what Nishad and Maya will find out about Mr. 
Nath, how they will discover it, and whether they will become friends. 
Sharing and Discussion: 
● Invite a few students to share their paragraphs with the class. 
● Provide feedback on the clarity and organization of their paragraphs, focusing on how well they 
structured their ideas. 
(NOTE: Encourage students to use their imagination while staying true to the text's themes and 
characters.) 
Independent Work (You Do)                       
Peer Review: Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner for 
feedback. 
● How would you describe Mr. Nath’s personality based on the story? 
● What was Nishad and Maya’s relationship with Mr. Nath at the beginning of the 
story? 
 
Closing                                                                                    
Today, we practiced writing well-organized paragraphs with clear topic sentences and 
supporting details. We explored Mr. Nath's character and predicted what might happen next in 
the story. 
 
Home Work 
Write a paragraph focusing on a different character or event from Expert Detectives. You can 
either continue the story or reflect on the perspective of another character. 
Period 12:  Poem (Mystery of the Talking Fan) 
Students will be able to identify and analyse the use of personification and figurative language 
in the poem. 
 
Hook:  
(NOTE: Walk into the room and look at a fan (or any classroom object) as if it's speaking.)

Say, Hey, Fan! What’s your opinion on today’s lesson?" or "Fan, do you have any advice for 
us before we start?" 
Exclaim: "Wait, did you hear that? The fan just said something to me! It says it’s ready for the 
lesson... but wait... I couldn’t hear exactly what it said!" 
 
Do you think fans can talk? (Take student responses) 
say, "In the poem we’re going to read today, a poet is sharing his imagination of fan actually

Experience and Reflection: 
Can you think of a time when you gave an inanimate(non-alive) object human-like qualities, 
like talking to your favourite gadget or comforting a stuffed animal? What did you say or

Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do)                      
Read the poem aloud to the students and ask the students to follow along as you read. 
The teacher facilitates a discussion using the questions on personification and figurative 
language in the poem. (Take student responses) 
● What does the fan represent in the poem? Does it convey any deeper meaning?      
● What would the poem be like if the fan weren’t personified?  
● How does personification effect the tone or mood of the poem? 
CFU (Open-ended/ Factual) 
Factual

2. “The car roared down the highway." What human trait is used here? 
Open-ended 
1. How does describing the fan’s noise as 'chatter' make you feel about the fan? 
2. What do you think the comparison of the night sky to coal tells us about the darkness? 
Group Work (We Do)                                   
The teacher divides the class into groups of 3-4 and asks them to read the poem in groups and 
identify and write more examples of personification and figurative language (simile, metaphor, 
etc.) in the poem. 
(OR)

Activity: Read the Short Passage Below and identify personification and figurative 
language. 
"The rain danced on the rooftop, tapping out a rhythm that sounded like music. The trees 
swayed gently in the breeze, whispering secrets to one another. Even the street lights flickered in 
time with the song of the rain, as if they were joining in the melody." 
Task 1: Identify Personification 
Underline the examples of personification in the passage. 
Write down what human trait is given to the object or thing. 
Your Turn: 
● "The trees swayed gently in the breeze, whispering secrets to one another." 
● Human trait given: _________ 
● "Even the street lights flickered in time with the song of the rain." 
● Human trait given: _________ 
Task 2: Identify Figurative Language 
Find one simile or metaphor in the passage. Explain why it is classified so. 
Your Turn: 
The rain danced on the rooftop, tapping out a rhythm that sounded like music." 
● "The trees swayed gently in the breeze, whispering secrets to one another." 
● Type of figurative language: ___________ 
● Explanation: ___________ 
Independent Work (You Do)                        
Answer the following questions.  
1. “Electrical his chatter" What human trait is given to the fan? 
2. “He ran as still as water", What human trait is given to the fan? 
3. "He ran as still as water", which is a figurative language used to explain it. 
4. “All the mystery was spoiled", what Type of figurative language is used and explained. 
Closing                               
Today, we learnt how personification gives human traits to objects, like a talking fan, and 
how figurative language, such as similes and metaphors, makes writing more engaging.
documents.subject: English

226 
Can anyone share an example of personification or figurative language from the poem we 
read? 
 
Home Work 
Read the Passage Below and complete task 1 and task 2. 
"The old house groaned under the weight of time. The windows stared out at the empty street 
like eyes, watching the world go by. The door creaked open, as if it were tired of being shut 
away. Outside, the wind howled like a wolf, angry and wild." 
 
Task 1: Identify Personification Underline the examples of personification in the passage. 
Write down the human trait that is given to the object or thing. 
Example: 
"The old house groaned under the weight of time." 
Human trait: Groaning (a sound people make when in discomfort) 
Explanation: The house is described as "groaning," suggesting it’s feeling the effects of time, 
as if it were a living being. 
Your Turn: 
● "The windows stared out at the empty street like eyes, watching the world go by." 
● Human trait given: _________ 
● Explanation: ___________ 
● "The door creaked open, as if it were tired of being shut away." 
● Human trait given: _________ 
● Explanation: ___________ 
Task 2: Identify Figurative Language (Simile/Metaphor/Personification) 
Find the figurative language used in the passage. Explain what the comparison means. 
Example: "Outside, the wind howled like a wolf, angry and wild." 
● Type of figurative language: Simile 
● Explanation: The wind is compared to a wolf, showing that it is loud and wild in its force. 
Your Turn: 
● "The windows stared out at the empty street like eyes, watching the world go by." 
● Type of figurative language: ___________

After revising the previous concept, do the given activity and ask students questions.

the board. Fold the triangle and draw a line. After 
folding the triangle, we get. Ask students what

Explain: Median of the triangle. 
The line we got after folding the triangle is called 
the median of the triangle. 
The median of a triangle is a line segment that joins one vertex to the midpoint of the opposite 
side of a triangle. 
The median of a triangle can be easily identified with the help of the following properties: 
● The median of a triangle is a line segment joining the vertex of the triangle to the mid-point of its 
opposite side. 
● It bisects the opposite side, dividing it into two equal parts. 
● The median of a triangle further divides the triangle into two triangles having the same area. 
● Every triangle has three medians, one from each vertex. The point of concurrency of these three 
medians forms the centroid of the triangle. 
● Each triangle median divides the triangle into two smaller triangles with equal areas. The 3 
medians divide the triangle into 6 smaller triangles of equal area.

Explain: Altitude of the triangle 
 The perpendicular line is called as altitude of the triangle. 
The altitude of a triangle is the perpendicular line segment drawn from the vertex to the side opposite 
to it. The altitude makes a right angle with the base of the triangle it touches. It is commonly referred to 
as the height of a triangle and is denoted by the letter 'h'.

After revising previous concepts, ask students to solve the given question. 
In a triangle, one of the exterior angles is 120°. The interior angle adjacent to this exterior angle 
is 45°. What are the other two interior angles of the triangle? 
Explain: Solving word problems 
Using the exterior angle property, the exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior 
angles. 
Exterior Angle = Interior Angle 1 + Interior Angle 2 
Given: 120°= 45°+ Interior Angle 2 
So, Interior Angle 2 = 120°−45°=75° 
The sum of the interior angles in a triangle is always 180°.  
Therefore: Interior Angle 3 = 180°−45°−75°= 60° 
So, the other two interior angles are 75° and 60°. 
And, The sum of all three interior angles is 180°  
x° + 50°+ y° = 180°     70°+ 50°+ y° = 180°     y° = 180°- 120° = 60°

After revising previous concepts, ask students given questions. 
Can we make the triangle using the given measurements without drawing?7 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. 
Explain: Property of the sum of the lengths of two sides of a triangle 
Yes, without drawing, we can find whether the given measurements make a triangle or not. 
The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side.  
The side cannot be less than the difference of the two sides.   
This property is also called the Triangle Inequality Theorem 
In the given example, measurements of three sides of the triangle are 7 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm 
Now, the sum of any two sides of the triangle should be greater than the third side. 
7 + 5 = 12 (Greater than third side) 
5 + 8 =13 (Greater than the third side). 
7 + 8 =15  (Greater than the third side). 
Thus, the triangle is possible with the measurements 7 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm

● Respiration is essential for survival of living organisms. It releases energy from the food. 
● The oxygen we inhale is used to breakdown glucose into carbon dioxide and water. Energy is released 
in the process. 
● The breakdown of glucose occurs in the cells of an organism (cellular respiration). 
● If the food is broken down with the use of oxygen, it is called aerobic respiration. If the breakdown 
occurs without the use of oxygen, the respiration is called anaerobic respiration. 
● During heavy exercise when the supply of oxygen to our muscle cells is insufficient, food breakdown 
is by anaerobic respiration. 
● Breathing is a part of the process of respiration during which an organism takes in the oxygen-rich air 
and gives out air rich in carbon dioxide. The respiratory organs for the exchange of gases vary in 
different organisms. 
● During inhalation, our lungs expand and then come back to the original state as the air moves out during 
exhalation. 
● Increased physical activity enhances the rate of breathing. In animals like cow, buffalo, dog and cat the 
respiratory organs and the process of breathing are similar to those in humans. 
● In earthworm, the exchange of gases occurs through the moist skin. In fishes it takes place through gills 
and in insects through the tracheae. 
● In a plant the roots take in air present in the soil. Leaves have tiny pores called stomata through which 
they exchange gases. The breakdown of glucose in the plant cells is similar to that in other living beings.

Author: Roald Dahl 
Summary: 
The story begins with Mr. Wonka explaining to Charlie how he invented a medicine called 
Vita-Wonk. He said he wanted to invent something that would make people older, unlike his 
earlier invention which made people young. So, he started thinking deeply and decided to find 
the oldest living things in the world to use in his new recipe. 
Charlie guessed that trees live the longest, and Mr. Wonk agreed. He said the oldest trees were 
Bristlecone Pines, found in Nevada, U.S.A., and they were over 4000 years old. 
Mr. Wonk then went on a journey in the Great Glass Elevator to collect things from very old 
creatures: 
Sap from a 4000-year-old tree 
Toenail clippings from a 168-year-old Russian farmer 
Egg from a 200-year-old tortoise

and he became a 75-year-old Oompa Loompa.

1. Dad and the Cat and the Tree (Poem) 
Poet: Kit Wright 
Summary: 
One morning, a cat got stuck in a tree. The narrator’s dad decided to rescue it himself. Although 
his wife warned him, he was confident and climbed up a ladder, but slipped and fell. 
Still determined, he tried again, this time climbing up a branch. But the branch broke, and he 
fell again. Not giving up, he climbed up the garden wall, and finally managed to reach the tree. 
But just then, the cat jumped down safely on its own! 
Ironically, the cat was safe, but the father got stuck in the tree instead! 
2 . Garden Snake (Poem) 
Poet: Muriel L. Sonne 
Summary: 
The poet shares that whenever he saw a snake, he would run away because he believed all 
snakes were dangerous. But his mother told him that some snakes are harmless and actually 
helpful as they eat insects.

Hook:  4 minutes 
Teacher dialogue: Imagine you are a scientist creating a potion that can make someone older 
instantly. What ingredients would you use? Maybe… wrinkled raisins? Ancient tree bark? A 
grandmother’s old sweater?(Give the students 30 seconds to think and call on a few students 
for answers.) 
Note: The teacher could also bring a few props like a small glass bottle with coloured water 
in it, a few old leaves etc. 
Experience and Reflection: Wow! Those sound like some powerful potions! But what if 
someone actually tried to create such a formula? In today’s story, Willy Wonka does just that—
but things do not go exactly as planned. Let us find out what happens! 
Explicit teaching (I do) 
 
 
 
Teacher action: The teacher uses a mix of Echo Reading and Supportive Reading strategies 
to discuss the text on page 168, ‘Mr. Willy Wonka begins…to Page. 168 ‘...from Peru.’   
Echo Reading: The teacher starts reading with proper stress, pause, and intonation, and the 
whole class repeats after the teacher.  
Supportive Reading: The teacher takes pauses at adequate intervals, gives the meaning of 
difficult words, and supports the children by analysing and explaining the text to understand it. 
Teacher Dialogue: Now, let us check. What is the problem with Wonka-Vite? Can somebody 
tell me? (Take student’s responses) 
● Yes! It made people so young that some disappeared. So, Mr. Wonka now needs to 
make a new invention that does the opposite. But how does he start? (Take student’s 
responses) 
(The teacher points to the lines where Mr. Wonka asks himself questions.) 
● Mr. Wonka is thinking like a scientist. He asks himself, ‘What is the oldest living thing 
in the world?’ This is important because real scientists also ask questions before making 
discoveries. But, of course, Mr. Wonka’s ideas are a mix of science and imagination! 
● Now, look at Charlie’s answer. What does he say? (Take student’s responses) 
● Correct! And Mr. Wonka agrees, but not just any tree. He talks about the Bristlecone 
Pine, a tree that is over 4000 years old. Imagine! A tree older than our entire city!

Teacher dialogue: (Post Guided reading) 
1. Why does Mr. Wonka collect things from the oldest living creatures? (Expected 
response: He believes they will help him create an invention that makes people older.) 
2. What is the effect of mixing all these strange ingredients together? (Expected response: 
He invents Vita-Wonk.) 
3. What happens when an Oompa-Loompa takes Vita-Wonk? (Expected response: He 
ages quickly and turns into an old man.) 
Teacher Explanation: This is a perfect example of cause and effect. Mr. Wonka wanted to 
reverse the effects of Wonk-Vite. So, he looked for very old things (cause) and created Vita-
Wonk (effect). But when someone takes Vita-Wonk (cause), they become much older 
immediately (effect). These connections are what we call cause-and-effect relationships. 
Now, let us practice identifying more cause-and-effect relationships in the story.

Teacher: Curiosity means always wanting to learn more and explore new possibilities. Willy 
Wonka is extremely curious about aging and reversing age. He does not just accept things as 
they are—he wants to test and discover new solutions.

Vita-Wonk!

● What does this show about Willy Wonka’s way of thinking?  (Take student’s responses)

a mistake with Wonka-Vite, but instead of quitting, he found a way to reverse the effects.

Hook 
Teacher action: Teacher walks into the classroom carrying a bag full of random objects (e.g., 
a toy car, a book, a small plant, a pencil, a ball). Teacher dramatically takes out the objects 
one by one and places them on the table. 
Teacher dialogue: Imagine I want to tell a story using these objects. But something is missing. 
If I only say ‘Car.Book.Plant.Pencil.Ball.’—does that sound like a real sentence? (Take student 
responses) 
What if I say, ‘The car zoomed past the book, nearly knocking over the plant, while the 
pencil rolled off the table and hit the ball’? 
Experience and reflection: What made the second version sound like a real story? What did 
I add? (Students may say: verbs, describing words, action, or full sentences.) Words have 
different jobs, just like we do in a classroom. Some name things, some show action, some 
describe. Today, let us revise how these different parts of speech work together to create 
meaning! 
Explicit Teaching (I do) 
Teacher Dialogues: Let’s refresh our memory! Parts of speech are categories that help us 
understand how words function in sentences. Do you remember the parts of speech we covered 
earlier? (Take student responses) 
1. Noun: A person, place, thing, or idea. Example: ‘The teacher loves freedom.’ 
2. Pronoun: Replaces a noun. Example: ‘She loves it.’ 
3. Verb: Shows action or state of being. Example: ‘The cat jumps.’ 
4. Adjective: Describes a noun. Example: ‘The happy child.’ 
5. Adverb: Describes a verb, adjective, or another adverb. Example: ‘She ran 
quickly.’ 
6. Preposition: Shows location/direction. Example: ‘The book is on the table.’ 
7. Conjunction: Connects words or phrases. Example: ‘I like tea and coffee.’ 
● Alright, now let us look at a sentence together and see how many parts of speech we 
can identify. I am writing a very special sentence on the board. Read it carefully and 
tell me what stands out to you (Take student responses)

Period 11: Grammar - Nouns 
LO: Describe distinguish and  use Common nouns, Concrete nouns, and Proper nouns.  
Explicit teaching (I do) 
Teacher dialogue: In the last two classes, we covered different parts of speech. Today let us 
explore different types of nouns. By the end of today, you’ll be able to describe and even draw 
examples of common nouns, concrete nouns, and proper nouns. 
● Common Nouns: Let us start with common nouns. Common nouns are general names 
for things. They don’t refer to anything specific. For example, if I say city—is that a 
specific place?(Expected response: No.)Right! City could mean any city, like Delhi or 
Mumbai. Other examples are words like teacher, river, and school. Can you give me 
some examples of common nouns? (Expected response: car, dog, or park.) 
● Proper Nouns: Now, let us talk about proper nouns. Proper nouns are special because 
they name specific people, places, or things. They always start with a capital letter. For 
example, India is a proper noun because it names a specific country. Can anyone tell 
me another proper noun? (Expected response: Hyderabad or Mr. Rao) Perfect! 
Hyderabad, Mr. Rao—these are all proper nouns. Remember, proper nouns are 
specific and always start with a capital letter.

Explicit Teaching (I do)   
Teacher dialogues: Every sentence needs a verb. Some verbs tell us what someone or 
something is doing—these are called action verbs. Do you remember any example? (Take 
student responses)  For example: 
● 
‘She writes a story.’ (Writes is the action.) 
● 
‘They dance beautifully.’ (Dance is the action.) 
● 
Other verbs do not show an action directly but help another verb. These are called helping 
verbs. For example: 
● 
‘She is writing a story.’ (Is helps writing to show the action is happening now.) 
● 
‘They are dancing beautifully.’ (Are helps dancing.) 
● 
Some common helping verbs are: is, are, have, has, was, were, will, shall. 
● 
Let us look at some more examples: Board Work (Examples): 
1. I play cricket. (Action verb: play) 
2. He is running fast. (Helping verb: is, Action verb: running) 
3. They have finished their work. (Helping verb: have, Action verb: finished)

Hook 
Teacher dialogue: Let us play a quick game! I will say two things, and you tell me which 
one is bigger. 
Teacher: An elephant or a mouse? 
Students: An elephant is bigger! 
Teacher: Which one is faster? Teacher: A cheetah or a tortoise? 
Students: A cheetah is faster! 
Experience and reflection: Great! You just compared things. Today, we will learn how to 
compare using special words—comparative and superlative degrees of adjectives and 
adverbs!  
Explicit instructions (I do) 
Teacher dialogue: Can someone remind me what an adjective is? (Take student responses.) 
● Very good! Adjectives describe nouns. When we compare two things, we use the 
comparative degree. For example, ‘Madhu is taller than Rahul.’ Here, taller is the 
comparative form of tall because we are comparing two people. 
● What part of speech is the word tall? (Take student responses.) 
● Examples on the board: smaller, brighter, faster, more interesting (comparative 
adjectives) 
● Write on board: Sarah is the tallest in the class.  
o What are we comparing Sarah with? (Take student responses) 
o Yes! The whole class. 
● When we compare three or more things, we use the superlative degree of the 
adjective. The word tallest is the superlative form of tall because we are talking about 
more than two people. 
● Examples on the board: smallest, brightest, most difficult, most interesting 
(superlative adjectives)/ most quickly, fastest (superlative adverbs) 
● Comparative words often end in -er, and superlative words often end in -est. But some 
words use more or most instead.

adjectives/adverbs we discussed.

Circulatory system in Animals: 
● The circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, and waste products within the body. 
● Blood consists of plasma, red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets. 
● RBCs contain haemoglobin, which helps transport oxygen. 
● WBCs play a role in fighting infections and protecting the body. 
● Platelets help in blood clotting to prevent excessive bleeding. 
● Blood vessels include: 
○ Arteries – Carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the body. 
○ Veins – Carry carbon dioxide-rich blood back to the heart. 
○ Capillaries – Facilitate the exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste. 
● The heart is a four-chambered organ that pumps blood continuously. 
● Heartbeats are the rhythmic contractions and relaxations of the heart muscles. 
● A stethoscope is used to measure heartbeats. 
● Pulse rate indicates heart activity and varies with physical exertion. 
Excretion in Animals: 
● The process of removing waste products from the body. 
● The human excretory system includes kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra. 
● Kidneys filter waste from the blood, forming urine. 
● Other excretory processes include sweating (removes salts and water) and exhalation (removes 
carbon dioxide). 
● Different animals excrete waste in different forms (e.g., fish release ammonia, birds excrete uric 
acid).

Transportation in Plants: 
● Root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil. 
● Xylem transports water and minerals from roots to leaves. 
● Phloem transports food (glucose) from leaves to other parts of the plant. 
● Transpiration (loss of water through leaves) helps pull water upward and cools the plant. 
● Stomata are tiny openings on leaves that control water loss and gas exchange.

Today, let us explore why transportation is so 
important!  
Activity 1:"The Traveling Water" 
Materials: 
● A dry sponge 
● A bowl of colored water 
● A clear straw (optional, for further 
demonstration) 
 Teacher (holding a dry sponge):  
This sponge is completely dry.  
● What do you think will happen if I place it 
in the water? 
(Dip the sponge in colored water and let 
students observe absorption.) 
 
● Now, does the water stay only where it first 
touched the sponge? 
(Gently 
squeeze 
the 
sponge.)
 
● What happens now? (Water flows out—
students see movement!) 
Right! Just like the water moved inside the 
sponge, the food and oxygen we take in, 
needs to move inside our body too. They 
travel to where they are needed. 
As we have learnt in the earlier classes, Living 
things cannot survive without essential materials 
like food, water, and gases. 
The food that we eat travels within the body.  
So, if food doesn’t stay in one place in our body, 
what do you think helps in transporting it? 
Great! Through blood. Just Imagine blood 
as a delivery service like Swiggy or Zomato. It 
carries oxygen and nutrients to all cells! 
In the same way, Food made in leaves is also sent 
to other parts of the plant about which we will be 
learning in the upcoming sessions.  
So, no living thing can survive without 
transportation! 
● Imagine if this system stopped for even a 
few minutes—what would happen?  
Exactly! That is why transportation is one of the 
most important processes keeping all living things 
alive.
Teacher divides the class into 
groups of four.

questions in your groups and 
analyze the role of transport

cities. Be prepared to share your 
thoughts with the class.

similar to delivery 
services in a city?

removal is just as 
important as transporting 
food and oxygen?

change?

So, the circulatory system has three main components: the Heart, Blood 
Vessels, and Blood! Today, let’s explore the importance of blood and its components!

Today, we learned that blood is made of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. RBCs carry 
oxygen, WBCs fight infections, Plasma transports nutrients, and Platelets help in clotting. Blood also travels 
through arteries and veins, keeping our body functioning. Next time you get a clot due to a small cut, 
remember—it’s your blood, specifically the platelets doing their job! And also we learnt about the importance 
of blood donation in saving others' lives.

Exactly! Platelets rush to the site of injury

So, blood is made of plasma, red blood 
cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Each 
plays a crucial role in keeping us alive and 
healthy. But did you know that donated 
blood can also help save lives? 
Many people need blood due to accidents, 
surgeries, or illnesses, but shortages are 
common. Voluntary blood donation is a 
safe and painless process that helps save 
lives. Hospitals and authorized centers 
store donated blood in blood banks for 
emergencies. 
There is no substitute for blood—when 
people lose it due to injury or medical 
conditions, transfusion is the only solution. 
Donating blood does not weaken the donor, 
and a small act of donation can make a 
big difference in saving lives. 
 There is no substitute for blood. If people 
lose blood from surgery or injury or if their 
bodies cannot produce enough blood, there 
is only one way to get it — through 
transfusion of blood donated by volunteers. 
Blood is usually in short supply. Donating 
blood does not decrease the strength of the 
donors.

SUMMARY: 
Recap of the period: The excretory system removes waste from the body, keeping it healthy. The kidneys filter 
blood and produce urine, which is stored in the bladder and expelled through the urethra. Other organs like 
the skin, lungs, and liver also help in waste removal. Sweating removes excess salts and cools the body, while 
the lungs expel carbon dioxide. Different animals excrete waste in different forms, like ammonia in fish and 
uric acid in birds. Proper excretion is essential to prevent waste buildup and maintain health.

As water escapes from the leaves, it

Transpiration is not just about losing

 It moves water to all parts of the

Summary: 
The chapter opens with Soumya’s letter to her friend Ananda, where she recalls their discussion 
on war and peace, and the sacrifices made by Indian soldiers for the country. Soumya shares 
her experience of visiting the National War Memorial in New Delhi on a school trip. She 
explains that the memorial was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and is dedicated 
to the brave soldiers who gave their lives for India. 
She describes the memorial’s structure: walls made of granite tablets, engraved with names of 
martyrs, and an eternal flame, the Amar Jawan Jyoti, which pays tribute to fallen soldiers. It 
was originally installed at India Gate in 1972 after the 1971 Indo-Pak war and was later moved 
to the War Memorial. 
Soumya tells about the four chakras (circles) at the memorial: 
Amar Chakra: Holds the eternal flame and a tall pillar. 
Veerta Chakra: Has six bronze murals depicting scenes of bravery.

Tyag Chakra: Granite walls with names of soldiers inscribed. 
Raksha Chakra: Trees planted around the memorial representing the protectors of the nation. 
She mentions medals of bravery like the Paramvir Chakra, Mahavir Chakra, Vir Chakra, and 
Shaurya Chakra. She shares the story of Major Somnath Sharma, the first recipient of the 
Paramvir Chakra, and Lance Naik Albert Ekka, whose story touched her deeply. 
Soumya also prepared a school presentation on Major Padmapani Acharya, who was martyred 
in the Kargil War of 1999 and awarded the Mahavir Chakra. He had written to his father 
quoting the Bhagavad Gita, saying one must fight with determination, whether to win or die 
with honour. 
In response, Ananda writes back expressing her happiness and pride. She shares her own 
memories of visiting a local war memorial in Chandigarh on Martyrs’ Day, and mentions 
Captain Anuj Nayyar, another brave soldier awarded the Mahavir Chakra. She praises the 
National War Memorial mobile app, available in 21 languages, and expresses a desire to visit 
it herself. 
She concludes the letter warmly, sharing her interest in stamp collecting (Philately) and 
remembering Soumya while eating idlis for breakfast. She ends the letter by sending regards 
to Soumya’s parents. 
 
 Meadow Surprises (Poem) 
Poet: Lois Brandt Phillips 
Summary: 
The poem describes the beauty and hidden wonders of a meadow. The poet says that if you 
observe closely, you’ll discover many surprises. Walking through the soft, velvety grass, 
listening to the sound of a brook, and watching a butterfly sipping nectar are all simple but 
joyful experiences. 
As you walk further, you might spot a rabbit hidden in the grass, which hops away when it gets 
scared. You may see a dandelion, which once was golden, now turned into a puffball ready to 
scatter in the wind. 
The meadow also hides many tiny homes: burrows in the ground, nests under tall grass, and 
ant mounds. The poem shows how nature offers surprises and beauty to those who look closely 
and appreciate it.

 Hook, Experience, and Reflection 
Hook:  
Show the image from the second slide of the PPT 
"Imagine you're holding an old, slightly crumpled letter. The ink has faded, but the words 
carry deep emotions. This letter was written by a young soldier, Captain Vijayant Thapar, 
just before he went into battle during the Kargil War in 1999. He was only 22 years old, full 
of dreams, but he knew he might not return. In his letter, he wrote heartfelt words to his 
family, especially to his parents, expressing his love, pride, and sense of duty to the nation." 
The teacher reads out the adjoining letter. 
 
Prompt Question (Think-Pair-Share) 
Why do you think soldiers leave behind letters like this before going into battle? 
Experience and Reflection: 
What emotions do you think a soldier feels while writing a letter from the battlefield? 
 
Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do) 
Imagine: "Close your eyes for a moment and imagine this scene. The sun is setting over a vast 
battlefield. A soldier stands, holding a pen in his trembling hands, writing his final words to his 
family. He knows he might not return, yet he writes with pride, not fear. His words are filled 
with love for his country and a promise to protect it at any cost." 
"Now, imagine the war is over. The battle has been fought, but many brave soldiers did not 
return home. Their families, their friends, and even people who never met them, gather to 
remember their sacrifice. Ask: But how do we ensure their stories are never forgotten? How do 
we honour their courage?  
Say: This is where war memorials come in." 
Watch: Let us watch a video on the National War Memorial. 
 Ask: In which city is the National War Memorial built?

Memorial was built and how it serves as a tribute to our soldiers." While reading try to connect

Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do) 
Recap and opening: “Last time, we explored the National War Memorial and understood why 
honouring our fallen soldiers is so important. But have you ever thought about how India honors 
soldiers who show great bravery, even in life-threatening situations? Today, we’ll investigate 
the highest gallantry awards given to such extraordinary heroes. Gallantry means “courage”. 
Explain: Let’s start with the Param Vir Chakra (PVC)—India’s highest military honor. It is 
awarded for the most exceptional bravery during war, often given after a soldier's death.  
Next is the Maha Vir Chakra (MVC), the second-highest gallantry award. It is given to soldiers 
showing great courage in battle. 
Then comes the Vir Chakra (VC), awarded for acts of valor on the battlefield.

from the President of India.

Recap and opening: “Previously, we learned about the bravery of Lance Naik Albert Ekka 
who sacrificed his life for the nation. But how do we, as a country, honour their sacrifice every 
day? One powerful symbol of respect is the Amar Jawan Jyoti, the ‘Flame of the Immortal 
Soldier.’ 
Today, we will explore what Amar Jawan Jyoti represents, why it was created, and how it 
connects to the memory of fallen soldiers.” 
Explain: It was the year 1971. India had just won a war against Pakistan, but that victory came 
at a great cost. Thousands of Indian soldiers had laid down their lives to protect the nation. Their 
sacrifice could not be forgotten. To honour them, in 1972, the Amar Jawan Jyoti was built under 
the India Gate in New Delhi. This eternal flame burned as a symbol of gratitude, courage, and 
remembrance. 
Watch: Let us watch a brief video on Amar Jawan Jyoti. (Timeline: 0 to 1 min) 
 Ask: What are your observations from the video?

visit….” from Page 119 to “..... stories of courage and valour” Page 120) and underline key 
phrases that explain its meaning.

Why was the Amar Jawan Jyoti merged with the National War Memorial?

Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do) 
Recap: "In our last lesson, we learned about the Amar Jawan Jyoti, the eternal flame that

from 1947 to today?”

PPT.  
Watch: Let us watch a brief video on the structure of the National War Memorial. (Timeline: 
1:22 - 3:33) 
Imagine: The teacher instructs the students to close their eyes and visualize the following 
situation: 
‘Imagine we are walking through the National War Memorial together. At every step, I will 
ask a quick question for you to think about!’ 
Step 1: Entering the Amar Chakra (Circle of Immortality) 
"We are now standing at the center. We see a flame burning endlessly.  
Q. What does this flame remind us of?"  
Explain: This is the Amar Chakra, where the flame represents soldiers who will always be 
remembered. 
Step 2: Moving into the Veerta Chakra (Circle of Bravery) 
"As we step ahead, we see huge illustrations. They show Indian soldiers fighting in battles.  
Q. Why do you think these illustrations were placed here?" 
Explain: This is the Veerta Chakra, a tribute to the valour of our armed forces. 
Step 3: Walking through the Tyag Chakra (Circle of Sacrifice) 
“Now, we see walls with thousands of names engraved. Imagine seeing the name of someone 
from your family here—how would you feel?" 
Explain: This is the Tyag Chakra, where the names of over 26,000 fallen soldiers are 
inscribed, honouring their sacrifice. 
Step 4: Reaching the Raksha Chakra (Circle of Protection) 
"Finally, we stand at the outermost circle. But instead of stone or metal, we see… trees! Why 
do you think trees surround the memorial?" 
Explain: This is the Raksha Chakra, symbolizing the shield of protection that soldiers 
provide.

LO: Students will be able to analyse how personal letters convey emotions and reflections 
about historical events. 
 
Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do) 
Ask: "Have you ever written a letter to share an experience that moved you deeply? How do 
letters help us express emotions differently than regular conversations?" 
Say: "Today, we will explore how personal letters convey emotions and reflections about 
historical events. We will first revisit Soumya’s letter to Ananda, where she describes her 
experience at the National War Memorial. Then, we will analyse how Ananda responds to her, 
showing how emotions evolve in written communication." 
Recap: 
● Where did Soumya visit, and what was the purpose of the place? (Expected Answer: She visited 
the National War Memorial, which honours fallen soldiers.) 
● What did she see at the memorial that made a deep impact on her? (Expected Answer: The 
eternal flame, the engraved names of soldiers, and the overall solemn atmosphere.) 
● How did she feel while standing in front of the memorial? (Expected Answer: She felt grateful, 
emotional, and reflective about the sacrifices made by soldiers.) 
● What did she want Ananda to do after reading her letter? (Expected Answer: She hoped Ananda 
would visit the memorial one day and experience the same emotions.)

Ask: "How do you think Ananda felt after reading Soumya’s letter? What kind of emotions 
might he express in his response?" 
Read: Now, let’s read Ananda’s letter and see how he reacts to Soumya’s words. Page 127-
128, “It was such a pleasure……..pay respect to the soldiers at the War Memorial.” 
Discuss: 
● How does Ananda’s tone compare to Soumya’s? (Possible answer: Ananda may feel inspired, 
thoughtful, or even emotional after reading the letter.) 
● What specific emotions does Ananda express? (Possible answer: Gratitude, admiration for 
soldiers, personal reflection on sacrifice.) 
● 
How did Soumya’s letter influence Ananda’s decision to join the army? (Possible answer: 
Reading about soldiers' bravery and sacrifice inspired her to serve the nation.) 
CFU (Open-ended/ Factual) 
Factual: 
1. What words or phrases in Ananda’s response show that she was inspired by Soumya’s 
letter? 
2. What decision did Ananda make after reading the letter, and why? 
            Open-ended: 
1. What emotions do both letters express, and how do they change between the first and 
second letters? 
2. What emotions do you think Soumya wanted to convey to Ananda in her letter? 
 
Group Work (We Do) 
● Divide the class into groups. 
● Each group will focus on a specific aspect of the letter 
● Group 1:  List three emotions expressed in the letter (e.g., fear, hope, pride). Discuss how 
do these emotions help us connect with the historical event by answering the following 
questions: 
How do these emotions show what the writer was feeling? How might people at that time 
have felt the same way? Can you think of a time when you or someone you know felt 
similar emotions? 
● Group 2: Identify three details in the letter that give insights into the historical event. 
Discuss how this letter helped us understand what happened during that time? 
● Group 3:  Choose two powerful sentences from the letter that express deep feelings. 
Discuss why these sentences stand out. How do they make the reader feel?

 LO: Students will be able to evaluate the significance of soldiers' sacrifices.  
 
Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do) 
Ask: "What do you think a soldier sacrifices for the country? Is it only their life, or is there more to

What Do Soldiers Sacrifice? 
● Personal Life – Soldiers spend months or years away from their families.

freezing mountains. 
● Health & Well-being – Many return with injuries or mental trauma.

Period:9 Reading Comprehension, segment -11(pg.202-pg.203) 
LO: Students will be able to examine the impact of war on soldiers and their families by    
reflecting on real-life examples and historical events. 
 
Explicit Teaching/Teacher Modelling (I Do) 
Ask (2 minutes): "How do you think war affects soldiers beyond the battlefield?" 
Explain: "War brings many challenges, not just for the soldiers who fight but also for their 
families. Let’s explore three major effects:" 
1. Physical & Emotional Toll on Soldiers 
● Many soldiers return with injuries or disabilities. 
● War also causes mental trauma (e.g., stress, fear). 
Ask: “How do you think a soldier feels when they return home after a long and difficult war? 
1. Sacrifices Made by Families 
● Families spend months or years apart from soldiers. 
● Worry and stress about whether their loved one will return safely. 
Ask: “How do you think families of soldiers feel while waiting for them to return?” 
2. Loss and Remembrance 
● Some soldiers do not return home, leaving behind grieving families. 
● Memorials and national days help honour their sacrifices.

Group Work (We Do) 
1. Divide the class into five groups. 
2. Each group will create four different sets of words where each set has one odd word. 
● Two sets should be based on meaning (e.g., categories like military ranks, bravery, war-
related objects). 
● Two sets should be based on grammar (e.g., verbs, adjectives, nouns, adverbs). 
3.  Groups will write down their four word sets with the odd one highlighted. Once ready, 
each group will take turns as quizmasters, presenting their word sets as a mini-quiz to the 
rest of the class. 
4. Other groups will try to identify the odd one out and justify why it doesn’t belong. 
5. The quizmasters will confirm the correct answer and explain the reasoning 
 
Independent Work (You Do) 
Below are four sets of words. In each set, one word does not belong. Identify the odd one 
out and explain why it doesn’t fit. 
1. Valor, Honour, Loyalty, Pistol (Odd one out: Pistol . Reason: All other words represent 
qualities of bravery, while "Pistol" is a weapon.) 
2. Parade, Ceremony, Battlefield, Tribute (Odd one out: Battlefield. Reason: All other 
words are related to honouring soldiers, while "Battlefield" is a place of war.) 
3. Command, Attack, Defend, Strategic(Odd one out: Strategic. Reason: All other words 
are actions in battle, while "Strategic" describes a plan or approach.) 
4. Courageously, Bravely, Quickly, Soldier(Odd one out: Soldier. Reason: All other words 
are adverbs describing how something is done, while "Soldier" is a noun.) 
5. Courageous, Tactical, Rifle, Brave(Odd one out: Rifle. Reason:  All other words describe 
qualities, while "Rifle" is a weapon.) 
 
Closing 
"Today, we explored how words can be grouped based on meaning and grammar, and we 
learned to identify the odd one out in different word sets. Just like in the real world, 
recognizing patterns helps us understand language better, think critically, and improve 
communication." 
"Can you think of a situation outside the classroom where identifying the odd one out might 
be useful?"

Ask : "When discussing a complex topic like war, how can we make our points clear and 
convincing? 
Explain : "A strong speaker organizes their thoughts and supports their ideas with examples. 
Let’s break this down into four steps using the OREO strategy.” 
O – Opinion (State your opinion clearly) 
"A good response starts with a clear opinion. For example: 
● ‘I believe wars happen mainly because of disagreements over land and power.’ 
● ‘In my opinion, wars are often the result of economic struggles and conflicts over 
resources.’" 
R – Reason (Give a reason to support your opinion) 
     "Strong speakers provide a reason to support their opinion. For example: 
● ‘Wars occur due to land disputes because countries want to expand their borders.’ 
● ‘Conflicts happen when nations fight over valuable resources like oil and water.’" 
E – Example (Provide an example to support your reason) 
"Strong arguments include historical examples to make them convincing. For example: 
● ‘The Indo-China War (1962) was fought because of a border dispute between India 
and China.’ 
● ‘The World Wars started due to conflicts over power and alliances among countries.’" 
O – Opinion Restated (Conclude by reinforcing your point) 
"We should restate our opinion to make our message strong and memorable. For example: 
● ‘This is why I believe wars happen when countries fight over land and power.’ 
● ‘In conclusion, conflicts over resources have always been a major cause of war.’" 
 
    CFU (Open-ended/ Factual) 
    Factual: 
1. What does the OREO strategy stand for? 
2. In the sentence, "I believe wars occur due to economic struggles," which part of the 
OREO strategy does this represent? 
    Open-ended: 
1. How does organizing your thoughts before speaking help you sound more confident? 
2. If you disagree with someone in a discussion, how can you express your point 
respectfully?

● Ask students to close their eyes and listen carefully. 
● Read aloud the following scenario in a calm, descriptive voice: 
“Imagine you are walking through a garden. The soft grass brushes against your feet. You 
hear a gentle stream flowing nearby. A butterfly lands on a bright yellow flower,. A rabbit 
suddenly hops away into the bushes.” 
Experience and Reflection: 
● After reading, ask: 
● What did you see in your mind?

detailed descriptions instead of just saying “a butterfly” or “a rabbit” in their 
poems?

words that help us "see", “hear”, and "feel" the grass.

        Meaning of rational numbers - Link 2   
● The teacher informs students that we will learn about rational numbers. 
 Explain: Meaning of rational numbers  
      The answers to the questions asked by students are: 
1) The whole numbers are the numbers without fractions and are a collection of positive integers 
and zeros. 
2) Integers are numbers that include all whole numbers (zero and positive numbers) and negative 
numbers. Integers do not include fractions or decimals. 
3) A fraction is a numerical value that is a part of a whole. 
4) The teacher said Sameera did not sort numbers correctly because -1/3  and -5/12 are not 
fractions. 
  So, what are -1/3 and -5/12 is? These are rational numbers. 
     A rational number is a number of the form p/q where p and q are integers, and q is not equal to 0. 
      For example : 5/6, 0.5, 3/7, -1/5 etc. 
 Then, what is the difference between rational numbers and fractions? 
 The main difference between rational numbers and fractions is fraction numbers cannot be negative. 
  Every rational number cannot be a fraction because when there are negative numbers, they do not fall  
      in the category of fractions such as - 1/2. 
       
 
Every fraction can be considered as a rational number.  
       
 
Every rational number cannot be considered a fraction. 
   A rational number is said to be positive if its numerator and denominator are both positive. 
    
 
For example: 1/5, 3/17, -16/-2 etc. 
  A negative rational number is a rational number that has a negative numerator or denominator.  
    
 
For example: -7/8, 5/-9 etc.

Convert 81/18 into standard form. What is the meaning of standard form? 
Explain: Standard form of a rational number 
A rational number is standard if the numerator and denominator contain no common factors other than 
1, and the denominator should have a positive integer. 
To convert a rational number into standard form we follow some steps. 
Step I: Obtain the rational number.  
 
Step II: See whether the rational number's denominator is positive. If it is negative, multiply or divide 
the numerator and denominator by -1 so that the denominator becomes positive. 
In 
,  the denominator is positive 
Step III: Find the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the numerator and the denominator. 
81 = 3 x 3 x 3 x 3 
 
 
18 = 2 x 3 x 3 
GCD = 3 x 3 = 9 
Step IV: Divide the numerator and denominator of the rational number by the GCD (HCF) obtained in 
step III. The rational number obtained is the standard form of the given rational number.

After revising the previous concept, ask students questions. 
Which number can we multiply in -8/9 to get 1, and which can we add in 1/6 to get 0? 
Explain: Additive inverse and reciprocal of rational numbers. 
An additive inverse is a number that results in zero on getting added to the original number. 
So, when we add -1/6 with 1/6 we will get the 0. 
The additive inverse of a negative number is positive, and the positive number is negative. 
For example, The additive inverse of -1/5 is ⅕ 
The reciprocal of a rational number is the result of switching the numerator and denominator of the 
number. 
For example: Reciprocal of 5/6  is 6/5 
So when we multiply the reciprocal of -8/9 we will get 1. 
-8/9 x -9/8 = 1 
The reciprocal of a number a (where aa is a non-zero rational number) is 1/a. Its reciprocal is 
always another non-zero rational number for any non-zero rational number. 
If we try to find the reciprocal of zero, we would look for 1/0, which is undefined. Division by 
zero is impossible in mathematics because there is no number that, when multiplied by zero, will 
give 1. 
A reciprocal of a rational number is always a rational number.

Summary: 
 
Reproduction 
● The process of producing new individuals from parents. 
Modes of Reproduction 
● Asexual Reproduction: New plants are produced without seeds. 
● Sexual Reproduction: New plants are obtained from seeds.

Example: Rose (stem cutting), Potato (eyes on tuber), Bryophyllum (buds on leaves).

animals, or even food!) . It grows super fast 
and reproduces in a special way called 
budding! 
Let us understand how yeast reproduce:  
(Shows a diagram or draws budding yeast 
on the board.) 
Look at this yeast cell. A tiny bump appears 
on it—this is called a bud. 
The bud grows bigger and bigger while still 
attached to the parent cell. 
Eventually, it separates and becomes a new 
yeast cell! 
Sometimes, multiple buds form, creating a 
chain of yeast cells. 
The new yeast cell is exactly the same as 
the parent yeast cell. There’s no mixing of 
traits from two parents—it’s an exact 
copy!" 
(Writes "Exact Copy = Clone" on the 
board.) 
This group of identical yeast cells is called a 
clone. A clone means a group of 
genetically identical organisms, all coming 
from a single parent. That’s why all the 
yeast cells look and behave exactly the 
same! 
● If one yeast cell doubles every hour, 
how many yeast cells will we have 
after 10 hours? 
(Encourage students to think about doubling: 
1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → ... until 1024.) 
See how fast clones can multiply? This is 
why yeast grows quickly!

Summary: 
 
● Spore Formation: Spores are released into the air and grow into new plants under favorable 
conditions. 
Example: Fungi, Moss, Ferns. 
Factual Questions: 
 
● What is called spore? 
● Give example for sporophyll? 
 
did it come from? 
(Waits for student responses.) 
Correct! It came from the air! The mold grew from 
tiny spores floating around us. Spores are like tiny 
seeds but much lighter. They travel through air, water, 
or even on animals until they land on something 
damp—like this bread! 
Do you know, Moss and ferns also reproduce using 
spores! Look at this fern leaf. See these tiny spots 
underneath? (Points to spore clusters in an image. 
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Xwx23dDdfk
PHdAAnx1BCJLVkaEAn33Ypb4TXg0DawyA/edit
?tab=t.0 ) 
These are spore-producing bodies, and they release 
thousands of spores into the air! 
If spores are so tiny and light, how do they spread to 
different places? 
Great! They spread by  wind, water, animals, etc. 
So, we learned that fragmentation helps algae 
multiply quickly, while spore formation allows fungi, 
moss, and ferns to spread over long distances—even 
in tough conditions!

How does spore formation help fungi reproduce? 
 
Open ended CFUs: 
Imagine a dry desert and a damp forest. Where do you 
think spores will grow faster, and why? 
How does fragmentation help algae spread quickly in 
ponds?
Groups share key observations 
and conclusions.
